subtopic: MR. GREGOIRE-ACCURACY OF STATISTICS RESPECTING UNEMPLOYMENT
MR. GREGOIRE-ACCURACY OF STATISTICS RESPECTING UNEMPLOYMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a question of privilege. It is a matter which, in my opinion, reflects on the rights of every member and those of the Canadian people. My question of privilege is directed to the Minister of Labour (Mr. MacEachen), and 1 regret that he is not in the house at the present time.
The statistics provided by the Department of Labour, and consequently by the Minister of Labour, concerning unemployment in Canada do not show the real situation.
In fact, we learned recently that in the province of Quebec there are as many unemployed people not registered on unemployment lists as there are registered. Therefore, it means that the number of unemployed would be twice the number given by official statistics. Now, the use of false statistics is likely to mislead hon. members.
I might have raised a grievance on that matter, but since the ministers and government members, in turn, refer to those statistics to praise the government and try to blot out the true situation, I thought it was appropriate to make it a question of privilege.
Therefore, I ask the Minister of Labour to see to it that his staff and officials give us the exact figures concerning the number of unemployed in the province of Quebec and all across Canada so that we will not be misled by the figures now provided to us and by the statistics as they are compiled.

speakeroldname: Hon. Mitchell Sharp (Minister of Trade and Commerce):
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I have just returned from the opening ministerial session of the Kennedy round of trade and tariff negotiations in Geneva. I ask the permission of the house to table the official text, in French and English, of the report adopted at the meeting.
Does the house grant permission?
Agreed.

Mr. Speaker, let me deal
briefly with the main decisions of the GATT meeting, particularly as they relate to Canada. First, the trade negotiating committee explicitly recognized that Canada is a country with a trade and economic structure such that the simple across the board formula for tariff negotiations would not yield reciprocity of benefit. The procedures for our participation have been agreed. Canada will begin the negotiations by offering concessions equivalent in value to the trade and economic benefits we may expect to receive.
Second, for the main industrialized countries, including the United States, the European common market, Britain and Japan, the working hypothesis will be an across the board cut of 50 per cent in their tariffs.
Third, it has been agreed that the exchange of offers will be made on September 10. Countries participating on the basis of across the board cuts will on that date notify the other negotiating countries of their list of exceptions to the general 50 per cent rule. Canada, on the other hand, will be starting from a positive list of offers of concessions. I confirmed that we are prepared to table our offer on the same date, September 10. Consultations with industry have been under way for some weeks during which hundreds of submissions have been received. I am confident that we shall be able to analyse these submissions and be in a position to table the Canadian offer on the agreed date.
Fourth, it was decided that for the countries participating on the basis of across the board cuts, exceptions are to be limited to a bare minimum required by overriding national importance.
As far as tariffs on industrial goods are concerned, these were the main decisions. The difficult question of disparities between

Report on GATT Meeting tariff levels and how to deal with them is not yet resolved. Nor has satisfactory progress yet been achieved with respect to procedures for the negotiation of agricultural products. As hon. members will see when they read the report I have just tabled, the ministers confirmed that the negotiations shall provide for acceptable conditions of access to world markets for agricultural products. While detailed negotiations have already been initiated with respect to wheat and other grains, the general rules and procedures for agricultural negotiations have yet to be worked out. Canada and other agricultural exporting countries expressed in strong terms their concern with this lack of agreement as to the treatment to be applied to agricultural products, and it was agreed that the necessary rules and procedures shall be established at an early date.
On the whole I believe this was a useful meeting. It committed the members of GATT to a timetable and to a number of procedures that should facilitate the forthcoming negotiations. Needless to say we did not resolve all our difficulties. Much remains to be accomplished even before September 10, and the subsequent negotiations themselves will probably last for many, many months beyond that date. Nor is this surprising, for never before has the world attempted such a far reaching attack on international barriers to trade.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the minister is to be congratulated on making his statement in the house, but not on the luminous nature of the statement. Indeed, I doubt whether I have ever heard a statement made in respect of a matter of such transcendent importance as trade as the one just made by the minister. Everything is postponed. Negotiations are to continue. Hope of ultimate success in some fields is held out. 'inis is a far cry on this sixtieth day of this session from the enthusiastic and optimistic statements made when hon. members opposite were in opposition about how simple the problem was going to be and how they were going to bring about an expansion and an extension of world trade.
In so far as agricultural products are concerned, I recall so well that when we were in power we were endeavouring to ensure the protection of Canada's position in the European common market. Those who now sit opposite were most critical of our stand in that regard. As agricultural exporters the reduction of tariffs on agricultural products is of prime importance to our country. Barriers against wheat imports are most important.
[Mr. Sharp.)
The minister has stated that no longer is the Liberal party-and this has been so for some months now-in favour of what it so strongly advocated when in opposition, namely a 50 per cent cut across the board in tariffs. It now has taken up the position which we had assumed; yet when we took the stand that a 50 per cent cut would be detrimental to Canada, more serious to Canada than possibly to any other country, the answer was that it could be done. In office hon. gentlemen opposite have found that what they advocated in opposition has been ineffective and has had to be retreated from.
Altogether, Mr. Speaker, I must say that the report is one of the most disappointing that the house has yet heard from the minister. In place of the optimism of the past there is today not even qualified optimism. There is uncertainty, if not a degree of hopelessness, which does not spell well for the future negotiations which will take place. All of us had hoped that out of this Kennedy round would come new expansion and development of trade; but certainly up to the present time, with the exception of platitudes and highest expectations, little or nothing has been done.

Mr. Speaker, I had not intended to comment on this matter, but in view of what the Leader of the Opposition has said perhaps I should say something. The minister is undertaking very delicate and difficult negotiations and it seems to me that it is a time for as little carping criticism as possible-
Oh, oh.

-in view of the very important nature of these negotiations and the vital effect which they will have on the future economy of our country.
I think the minister has given us a note of cautious optimism this afternoon. There are circumstances in connection with these talks which were not in evidence at Brussels, but at the same time we still do not know what the French are up to and we do not know what the Germans are up to.
We do not know what you are up to.

But I know what you are up to, and I think by this time all of Canada knows what you are up to.
We do hope that as the talks proceed the minister will be able to resolve one of the most vital problems which, of course, is the problem of agriculture. Although at the moment there seems to be no clear indication where the talks are going on the whole, as I have said, we are glad to have this report and we hope that as negotiations proceed some of the more difficult aspects can be

resolved so that future reports will contain something a little more concrete which we can discuss.

Mr. Speaker, I think we can all agree that the announcement the Minister of Trade and Commerce has just made in respect of new negotiations on world trade and commerce concerns probably the most ambitious undertaking the world has ever known to reduce tariffs in all fields. We are disappointed, of course, that there has not been more progress that could be announced at this date. We are particularly disappointed at the indication in the minister's speech that there was almost no progress in resolving these problems relating to trade in agricultural products.
I want to say to the minister, however, that we hope this problem does not get blown up to such magnitude it prevents progress in other fields. We know from the past few months that there have been some very serious ramifications in other relationships between countries because this matter of agricultural trade is one in which emotion runs very high. We hope there will be, as I said, more progress, and we would not like to see these discussions bog down so that progress is prevented in other fields.
We are also a bit apprehensive about the package or packages the minister intends to offer on September 10. We hope he has communicated sufficiently with all the industries involved and has, in fact, received some approval and co-operation or promise of cooperation from them so that we do not have a situation in which one segment of our industry is going to be sacrificed or partially sacrificed to the advantage of some other segment.
There is one other point I should mention, and that is this matter of some new and more workable means of international settlements. We believe this is a most important new departure in world trade that needs to be developed, and while the minister did not say anything about it in his statement today we hope Canadians are leading the discussions in attempting to arrive at some new and more workable means of making these international settlements.

Mr. Speaker, we are happy to see that the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Sharp) has returned safe and sound from the Geneva conference. We listened very closely and have noted that he stated that various countries in the world are trying to improve their respective economic standards of living.
We find that every country is looking for foreign markets, in other words they are
Sale of Wheat to Red China trying to increase their exports as much as possible and, to help them, it is announced that certain tariff barriers between those various countries are being removed.
Shortly, at another meeting, another deci-cision will be taken on September 10, but to date I think few changes were made in regard to imports or exports or in regard to trade with other countries.
Every country has to cope with an overabundance of goods and products, and they all are seeking exterior outlets, while neglecting the domestic market.
When he was in Geneva the minister certainly realized that all countries have to face the same problems. We all have products to export. There are certain financial obstacles which threaten smoother relations between countries, as there are financial obstacles inside this and other countries which impair the disposal of existing goods, and preventing satisfaction of our domestic needs.
I ask the minister when he returns to Geneva, to suggest in turn to all those countries that they control or settle their own domestic problems. Then we shall see that the international question will be much more easily settled. Yet this way we shall not only assist our farmers, but our businessmen and industrialists as well and improve our economic system, because we shall help our own people first, which is what we want to do. speakeroldname: Hon. Mitchell Sharp (Minister of Trade and Commerce):
maintopic: WHEAT-ANNOUNCEMENT OF FURTHER SALE TO RED CHINA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise with some diffidence to make another announcement and I do hope this one will not disappoint the Leader of the Opposition as much as my previous announcement apparently did.
The Canadian wheat board is announcing in Winnipeg today that under the provisions of the second long term wheat agreement with China a further sales contract has been signed to provide for the export of 1,075,000 long tons, 5 per cent more or less, of wheat of which one million tons will be shipped from Pacific coast ports during July to December and the balance of 75,000 tons from St. Lawrence river ports during the period May through December, 1964. Assuming the full tolerance is taken, this amounts to slightly over 42 million bushels.
Including the sales contract covered by this announcement, total sales under the second long term agreement amount to 2.1 million tons or approximately 77.4 million bushels. As in the previous sales contracts, payment terms for sales under the long term agreement are 25 per cent cash when each vessel is loaded

Harbour Commissions
and the balance of 75 per cent in 18 months with interest. The deferred payment provision is made possible by a guarantee to the Canadian wheat board by the government of Canada.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING REPLACEMENT OF CHIEFS OF STAFF COMMITTEE

speechtext: The house resumed, from Friday, May 7, consideration of the motion of Mr. Hellyer for the second reading of Bill No. C-90, to amend the National Defence Act.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING REPLACEMENT OF CHIEFS OF STAFF COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to take the time I have left to deal mainly with two suggestions resulting from the statement made last Friday by the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Hellyer) on the plan now being studied.
First, I think it should be pointed out that the people most directly affected do not seem too happy about the proposals set forth by the minister to compensate the members of the armed forces who will be discharged following the re-organization of the general staff and the armed forces.
Indeed, last week and Saturday in particular, newspapers reported some rather bitter comments made by members of the armed forces or their representatives.
When he replied to a question put by the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Diefenbaker) this afternoon, the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) did not seem aware of the representations and of the fully justified objections made against those decisions.
I feel that those decisions are open to criticism on two counts.
With regard to the government's intention to fully assess the amount of the compensation paid to discharged personnel, I find somewhat strange the intention to tax those allowances paid to the personnel, because a tax is being levied as if it were an income. In this case, it is not an income, but a sum of money, an

allowance paid for a specific purpose. That aim is to ensure or facilitate the rehabilitation of military personnel.
It is easy to understand that those soldiers, seamen or airmen, who have served for a number of years in the armed forces, need special provisions to enable them to adjust to civilian life, when they could normally expect, under the terms of their enrolment, to serve the rest of their active life in the armed forces.
That makes me wonder why such a sharp distinction is made between the various ranks of military personnel. Thus, a general with 15 to 20 years' service in the armed forces can expect to get a compensation or gratuity that can amount to several thousands of dollars, whereas an ordinary soldier with the same length of service will receive only a small fraction of that amount.
Yet, would it not be reasonable to think that it would be much more difficult for a private, who perhaps has no trade and surely no savings and few business connections, to rehabilitate himself than it would be for a general who received a very high pay while serving in the armed forces?
Therefore, it seems to me that if the minister intends to pay certain gratuities to discharged personnel for rehabilitation purposes, no distinction should be made on the basis of rank. Both the private and the general gave their time and perhaps sacrificed another career to serve their country and, surely, if for some reason or a policy change they are forced to leave the armed forces and look for a civilian job, no distinction should be made because, after all, such distinctions are only factitious.
Consequently, I move on the one hand, that the compensation paid to officers and servicemen who are forced to retire be income tax free, and, on the other, that the amount of the compensation be allowed to vary according to the number of years of service but not according to the grade of the individual concerned. In addition, I suggest that the compensation be graduated according to the person who retires.
Finally, I believe that the government should take special steps, perhaps along the lines followed after the last world war, to enable retired members of the armed forces to take special courses or learn a trade to facilitate their rehabilitation.
Oftentimes, servicemen, in the army, the air force or the navy, learn a trade which is useless to them once they return to civilian life and, if we want to be really fair to them -and however stirring the minister's call- we must make all these benefits available to these men who are the innocent victims of a

policy change, a change that may be necessary but which is nevertheless a government policy change which vitally affects them as well as their families.
And now, Mr. Speaker, I wish to close my remarks with these few words on the defensive role that Canada should play today. First of all, it should be a role proportionate to the means of our country.
Following the minister's statement it was reported in the press that as a result of these changes a saving of $10 billion was expected during the next ten years. I think that the minister should correct the wrong impression given by his remarks, because after considering them closely one realizes that it will not really be a saving but simply a transfer of certain sums from military personnel or the administration to development of military equipment.
I feel that our country should refrain from trying to play the part of a great power, and especially all parts at the same time. I submit that the efforts of our country should be restricted to the development of an efficient military technology which would give our country the opportunity to equip itself with modern weapons, and this could make all the difference between an obsolete and an adequate defence.
Mr. Speaker, today, the part played by the great powers cannot be determined by the population of a country or even by its resources. There are countries with a very large population which, however, are not great powers. There are some nations with huge natural wealth, which are not among the great powers. For instance, there are India and Brazil, with vast resources and a huge population, but undeveloped yet which do not count among the really great powers in today's accepted meaning of the words.
At the same time, there are some countries with a comparatively small population which, thanks to their very advanced technological achievements, rank among the great powers, like the United Kingdom, which is not among the most populated. There are also France and Germany, instances of highly industrialized nations, with a highly developed industrial potential and a very progressive military technology, which are able to play a key part in international relations.
After all, we just have to think that a country has only to discover a new means of destruction, perhaps a biological or chemical means of warfare, or some death ray, to become a great power. It is a good illustration of the need for Canada to penetrate further into the field of technological and military research.
National Defence Act
The minister will admit that, at this time, our country does not make a very marked effort in that direction, and that nothing in the minister's statement implies that the situation will soon be remedied. Because of its refusal to face the need of stressing military research this country will only be a second class nation as long as no decision is taken to the contrary.
I think the minister should show some courage, go ahead and correct that alarming situation.
Mr. Speaker, it would seem that Canada should further direct its efforts towards the setting up of a mobile peace force which would immediately be trained jointly with other nations and put at the disposal of the United Nations organization.
There is, I think, a field where Canada can play a most efficient part, best suited to its way of thinking and its history.
I know that the Prime Minister raised the question. He spoke of negotiations which had started, or were about to start with certain countries to work out this peace force. Well, we would like to have more specific information in this respect. Would the minister tell us how the project could take shape from a military point of view and be integrated in the defence effort of this country.
Speaking about that peace force, I cannot help but think of the situation now prevailing on Cyprus. I believe that if there is now a need to establish a peace force, it is in order to prevent a situation such as the one that occurred and is developing now on the island.
We would have a great many questions to ask the Minister of National Defence regarding the situation of our troops on the island of Cyprus. For instance, we should like to know whether the Canadian contingent is there under the auspices of the United Nations? That question comes to mind, because we do not know to whom the commander in chief of the Canadian force is really responsible.
Moreover, we do not know whether the countries which promised to send a contingent to set up that force will soon keep their promise, because of all the countries which promised to send forces, only Canada has fully carried out its commitment. Up to now, the other countries which had committed themselves to increase the strength of the force have only sent token forces, so that only Canadian and British soldiers make up this peace keeping force.
The conclusion must be reached that instead of being a United Nations force, this force is jointly administered by Canada and

National Defence Act
the United Kingdom, whereas the government, and more particularly the Prime Minister, had informed the house of quite definite and specific commitments in this regard. In fact, the Prime Minister stated that this contingent would not be sent to Cyprus, unless it really and effectively constituted a force under the control of the United Nations.
We are led to ask that question by the fact that the United Nations are not responsible for the expenses of the contingent, since Canada itself will assume that burden.
In addition, I think that the minister should give us the assurance that every arrangement has been taken for the security of the Canadian troops now in Cyprus. And still again I blame the government, the Minister of National Defence and the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Martin) for refusing to disclose the security arrangements essential for our Canadian troops as well as instructions which have been given to them.
I believe that the Canadian people are concerned about the security of our troops in Cyprus, and they wonder also as to the part they are playing there now and will be playing in future.
I am of the opinion that Canada was willing to send a peace force to Cyprus provided its real mission would be to restore peace under the auspices of the United Nations. Up to now, we have not received any assurance from the Minister of National Defence or other ministers in that respect. That is why I say that the minister should take this opportunity, when the whole matter of our defence can be considered, to explain to us the role played by our troops in Cyprus, and especially the security measures taken to ensure their survival and welfare.
In my opinion, if the minister wants to tackle resolutely the problems which we, on this side of the house, have pointed out to him, and if he really wants to give us adequate answers, he will show that he is a great Minister of National Defence, a role he would like to assume and I wish him well. But, up to now he has not proven he could play such a role. So we will be waiting very impatiently for his answers before the end of this debate.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING REPLACEMENT OF CHIEFS OF STAFF COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to take the opportunity offered by the debate on setting up a special defence committee to make a few observations.
Some time ago, the minister announced some rather drastic reforms concerning the Canadian armed forces. He informed the house that General Walsh had been appointed chief of the general staff. In this connection, I

would like to ask the minister if he is considering giving a special status to General Allard, whose services are highly appreciated within the Canadian armed forces. General Allard could definitely assume greater responsibilities than those he now has, and he would have a part to play if he were associated with General Walsh and jointly in charge of the Canadian armed forces general staff.
Mr. Speaker, I think my suggestion is constructive since it is very difficult for only one man to have complete responsibility over the general staff of Canadian forces. I think that if the minister and the government placed their reliance in General Allard, he could work in co-operation with General Walsh. In fact, those two highly qualified men could do a better job in the interest of the Canadian armed forces.
On many occasions we heard the hon. member for St. Jean-Iberville-Napierville (Mr. Dupuis), now Minister without Portfolio, discuss before us the College Militaire Royal de Saint-Jean. Several hon. members on this side of the house also spoke on that matter and if I refer to pages 249 and 250 of Hansard of January 22, 1960, I find a plea made by the hon. member for St. Jean-Iberville-Napierville asking that the College Militaire Royal de Saint-Jean be put on the same footing as the Kingston Royal Military College and asking that it be given a complete four-year course.
Mr. Speaker, the present government has now been in office over a year. That pledge to establish a four-year course was made by the hon. member for St. Jean-Iberville-Napier-ville specially during the last election, and I am wondering what the government is doing in that field.
I wonder what the government proposes to do, if it intends to ignore the oft-repeated request made by the hon. member for St. Jean-Iberville-Napierville. Besides, as I said a little earlier, the hon. member spoke about that during the last election campaign. I wonder what the minister proposes to do. Why did he not tell the house that the course would be complete and on the same footing as the one in Kingston? Has the minister lost faith in the hon. member for St. Jean-Iberville-Napierville, Minister without Portfolio? Does the minister want us, on this side of the house, to rise every day to alert public opinion and indirectly force the government to act?
In my opinion, it is important that the minister tell us what he proposes to do and if he intends to put that college on the same footing as the one in Kingston. Besides, the government has received numerous requests from members belonging to our group, from

Saint-Jean-Baptiste societies and organizations in the province of Quebec, and even in other provinces, to the effect that the course given at the St. Johns Royal Military College should be complete like the one given in Kingston.
This would not exclude the possibility of exchanging students, that is French speaking students could go to Kingston and English speaking students could continue their course at the St. Johns Royal Military College. I believe such a policy would contribute greatly towards national unity.
Mr. Speaker, according to newspaper reports published recently, many Canadian servicemen have made requests to appear before the Laurendeau-Dunton commission in order to state their grievances. The minister announced that he would allow military personnel to submit briefs to the royal commission on biculturalism and bilingualism provided that it be done behind closed doors so as to avoid political controversy.
Mr. Speaker, I should like to point out that according to the press Professor Arsene Lau-ziere, of the Royal Military College in Kingston, stated that there exists some discrimination against French Canadians at present with respect to promotions within the Canadian army. I feel that such a charge on the part of a professor at the college in Kingston is very serious, because it raises doubts in the minds of Canadians and contributes to disunity in our country.
It is all very well to allow servicemen to explain their grievances to the royal commission on biculturalism, but this does not settle the problem in my opinion, since this investigation may last a year or two and the government will not in the least be bound by the commission's recommendations.
In view of the serious charges made by an official of Kingston Military College and others, I ask the minister whether an investigation could be made within the armed forces, so as to clear up the situation and check whether this professor's statements are true. The minister cannot overlook the serious charges which have been raised. It seems to me that even if the government allows servicemen to explain their grievances to the Laurendeau-Dunton commission, it will not be bound to take action. The only way would be a royal commission which would call witnesses and take action to correct the situation, if there is really discrimination in the armed forces. That is the only way-and there is no other, Mr. Speaker-to remove any doubt in the minds of the Canadian people.

Mr. Speaker, I would be very happy to have the opinion of the minister on that matter.
On the other hand, I have always been concerned about something which has respect to the Canadian forces in NATO. I should like to know whether food and material for the Canadian forces in NATO come from Canada or are supplied by the United States and England. I was told that it was very difficult, in view of the small number of Canadian soldiers now in Europe, as compared to American and English forces, to organize a system to supply the Canadian armed forces with provisions coming from Canada. But I wonder if it would not be possible for the Canadian government to come to an agreement with the United States and England in order to get some compensation. For instance, we might have a special quota; Canada might sell to the United States and England a certain amount of farm products.
The minister knows that we have farm surpluses in Canada at the present time. Canadian farmers-especially those in eastern Canada-are faced with a serious crisis which jeopardizes the Canadian economy because if the citizens of a part of Canada do not have an adequate yearly income, by the same token, the other part of Canada suffers therefrom.
I wonder if it would not be possible to review our agreements completely, so that we Canadians will not be left holding the bag, and so that we will obtain some compensation on the part of the American and British governments.
Mr. Speaker, the Canadian people are presently worried about the situation now developing in Cyprus and about the fate of their troops. We do not know whether Canadian troops will remain three months, three years or five years in Cyprus; the way things are going, these troops will likely have to stay there at least five years. We hope the government will ask authorization from parliament, after the three months' period has expired, to see whether it will agree to extend the stay of Canadian troops in Cyprus.
There appears to be some confusion at this time. What is most unfair, in my opinion, and what completely destroys the authority of the United Nations, is that the Canadian people are obliged to pay the entire cost of their troops' stay in Cyprus. Normally, this expense should be divided among all the member countries of the United Nations. There are some countries, for instance, France and Russia, which, in the past, refused to pay their contribution to the United Nations.

National Defence Act
Those same countries have exactly the
same right to vote as those who carry out their commitments, such as Canada and the United States.
It is absolutely necessary, at the very next session of the United Nations, that the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Martin) call upon the secretary general of the United Nations to urge the United Nations, that the cost of the Canadian troops on Cyprus should be paid by them and not only by the Canadian people.
The Canadian people are prepared to do their share for peace, but they do not want, in other words, to be taken in as regards every conflict throughout the world. We have done more than our share to assist the United Nations financially. It is only fair and reasonable that the government, through the Secretary of State for External Affairs, should take a definite stand at the next session of the United Nations.
Normally, the next session of the United Nations should begin in September, but because of the American elections, it will be postponed until November. I hope that the Canadian government will take a definite position in that matter. We are prepared to do our share but we do not want to bleed ourselves white only to be laughed at. We have obligations at home. Unemployment here is startling. In Canada we have 600,000 unemployed. We are prepared to co-operate for peace, but with logic and common sense.
I should like to ask the Minister of National Defence a few questions concerning our Canadian troops on Cyprus. I have it on good authority, from a trustworthy informant, as it was given to me by the very friends of the minister.
I ask the minister the following question.
The most alarming rumours are circulating in Cyprus and in well-informed diplomatic and military circles, with regard to the relations, between General Gyani and a Greek personality in the Cypriot cabinet on the one hand, and Mr. Tuomioja and his assistant, Mr. Millar, on the other hand, which might, according to some reports, in the long run compromise the success of the peace operation and more particularly the position of the force. Those rumours, of which I was informed by a reliable source, left me in the deepest state of alarm. Yet, I would hesitate to give full particulars- though my information is rather specific- before the minister tells us whether my authority is authentic and reliable.
I would like to know, for instance, whether the rumours with regard to the personal relations of General Gyani are well-founded. What is the background of

Mr. Millar, and in what way does he assist Mr. Tuomioja? Are the U.N. authorities and the Canadian government fully aware of the situation and of the possible influence the Canadian contingent might wield to make peace prevail?
Second, could I be told whether the Turk-ish-Cypriot authorities were warned by the U.N. command, according to the terms of reference conferred by Mr. U Thant, of the large scale operations launched by Greek Cypriots against the fort of St. Hilarion? Because, according to other well-founded rumours, the Turkish authorities had not been advised as they should have been, and, knowing that those operations could not have escaped the supervision of the Canadian military personnel, they are said to have tried to shift the blame onto the Canadian soldiers.
I believe, Mr. Speaker, that these allegations are quite serious. It would be most important for the minister to examine this situation and obtain the required information, in order to clear this up before the house and to reassure the people of this country who, as I said, have accepted to send a Canadian contingent to Cyprus and, furthermore, who are paying the full cost thereof.
In closing my remarks, I am asking the minister again: How is the Canadian contingent in Cyprus supplied with food and equipment? It would be most important that the Canadian farmers should not be the losers, and I would be very happy if the minister could consider these suggestions in order to make a report to the house, in the interest of the Canadian taxpayer.

speechtext:
am very sorry I was not able to be here last Friday when an introductory statement was made on the second reading of this bill. But I am certain, Mr. Speaker, you will realize that when a member of this house is 3,000 miles away from his home city and only takes some two days off in three months to revisit his family and constituents, he is not abusing his position as a member of the House of Commons. Unfortunately, it would be just in those days I took to return to the city of Vancouver that the questions as to the reappointment of the defence committee and second reading of this particular bill came up.
I have only had a few moments in which to glance over the introductory statement made by the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Hellyer) and other statements last Friday, but even so I feel I would like to take a few minutes in which to make some comments.

First, I should like to express my bitter disappointment at the long delay in reappointing the special committee on defence. When this committee brought in its report at the close of the last session there were some 13 important matters which were taken to be of such major seriousness that the committee felt it should be reappointed at an early date in order to deal with them. Had the committee been reappointed early in the present session it could have been investigating these most important matters. We have lost two valuable months. In addition, had the committee been reappointed earlier, the white paper brought down by the Minister of National Defence could have been referred to it immediately for consideration, and by now it could have been the subject of a month's study. I do not know why the committee was not reappointed immediately, especially in view of the importance attached last session to its early establishment. I can only express the hope that the delay was not due to a deliberate act of government policy. I do not think it was the deliberate intention of the Minister of National Defence to delay it. But somebody did, and I only hope that whoever held it up did not do so with the intent of preventing the committee from having sufficient time in which to do the necessary job of studying Canada's defence policy now and in the future. I may say, though, that I am a little suspicious.
I am also disappointed, in view of the agreement that the appointment of the committee last Friday would go without debate but that there would be opportunity during the discussion of this bill for a broad and comprehensive debate on any aspect of defence, that the Minister of National Defence did not give more information to the house -than he did last Friday. It appears he did what is normally the correct thing to do, that is, he stayed strictly within the principles of the bill before us. But because of the understanding that there would be an opportunity for a broad discussion on defence I had hoped he would have gone into greater detail about some of the most important questions which face us. First, I think he should have given the house an explanation for changes made in government policy since the end of last session. This was not done and I think it was unfair to members of the House of Commons, who should not have to rely upon what appears in newspapers when they see explanations of these matters. Surely, the house should be told in detail the reasons for any changes in government policy made between the end of last session and the time the minister made his speech the other day. I will return to this in a moment.
National Defence Act
I wish now to make mention of the bill before us and the statement by the minister, which I read in the newspapers, about the proposals being made on behalf of those who will be leaving the service because of integration of staff or other changes in policy. As I read the statement of the minister it was based wholly on the making of a cash payment the extent of which was to depend upon the period of service-ten months, and so on-

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING REPLACEMENT OF CHIEFS OF STAFF COMMITTEE
speechtext: Plus a waiving of the pension penalty.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING REPLACEMENT OF CHIEFS OF STAFF COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Plus certain waivers. I wish to express my extreme regret that this was the only plan considered, or at least that it was the only one proposed. I am in receipt of communications from men in the forces who may be affected. I have heard from one air force base in particular. I am told that after consideration of this matter those who think they might be affected are not so much concerned with receiving a settlement of perhaps ten months' pay on discharge as they are with being readapted into civilian life. In other words, Mr. Speaker, according to the letters sent to me by those in the forces at the present time, they would have preferred an option to this effect, that on their discharge the Department of National Defence or any other department that might be brought into it would see that they receive training in order to readapt them into civilian life, as well as being compensated, of course, on being discharged from the forces for their maintenance during training.
This point in particular was brought to my attention, that the taxpayers of Canada have over the years paid thousands of dollars to train men in individual trades in the navy, the air force and the army. Therefore they have a basic understanding and a thorough knowledge of those trades for military purposes. They say, "Why could we not, then, have the department give us on discharge, or pay for us to undertake, the additional training so we may adapt to civilian occupations what Canada has paid for us to learn for military purposes?" If I had received only one letter on this subject, Mr. Speaker, I would not have raised it, but I have received a number of letters from two of the bases which think they will be affected. According to my information, the majority of men would prefer this kind of treatment on discharge to the $3,000, $4,000, $5,000 or $8,000 they will receive by way of gratuity.
As this information comes from the armed services perhaps there is still time for the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Hellyer) to give consideration to this additional approach to caring for those in our armed forces whose

National Defence Act
services may no longer be required in June, at the end of the year, or next year. I think it is a suggestion that is most worthy of consideration by the minister, and is most worthy, Mr. Speaker, coming from these men in the armed forces who say this is what they would prefer; that is, being retrained instead of getting something which may last them for a year or, as was pointed out to me, they may invest it stupidly in a small business, go broke and have nothing. Therefore I hope the minister will consider this proposition put forward by the men themselves, of training for readaptation from military service into civilian occupation.
Now, sir, may I spend a little time on the general principles of defence. I will not deal with this subject in detail because, as I said, I have not had time to go through everything that was said last Friday. I believe the Minister of National Defence did a disservice to this House of Commons in his statement of Friday in not bringing us up to date on the Canadian position, in view of the dissertations and discussions of recent weeks relative to NATO, particularly in regard to Canada's position in NATO relating to all the conflict which, if the newspapers are correct, is now developing. I refer in particular to the position of France toward NATO in view of the de Gaulle policy. If the newspapers are correct, the position taken in the past two or three weeks due to the de Gaulle policy is this: He has pulled out his naval officers because he is not satisfied, and we read of the additional emphasis he is putting on his being the power-this is the only basis upon which you can put his policy-in Europe. In view of this, the house was entitled to know last Friday, not in the future, what the position is, in view of the discussions and dissertations in Europe of the last few weeks, particularly with regard to NATO. We are entitled to know what is the view of the Minister of National Defence and the government on this matter. In particular I think we should have had a detailed answer as to why we are still maintaining air force squadrons in France.
Mr. Speaker, I think it is-I have said it before and I repeat it-absolutely and positively ridiculous and asinine to have a government policy whereby France has its air force to some extent in Germany so they can have nuclear warheads, while we maintain squadrons in France that cannot be similarly equipped. I am against nuclear weapons, but on this facet of the question I cannot understand the stupidity of government thinking, and I cannot understand why the Canadian taxpayer should have to pay to maintain those

squadrons in France when France is challenging the very basis of NATO and the cooperative influence and control of NATO. To my mind this just does not make sense. It has not yet been explained; perhaps it will be explained in the defence committee when it meets.
Also, Mr. Speaker, in recent weeks in particular statements have been made by statesmen of the world to the effect that if there is a war in the future-and thank heavens there seems to be a diminution of that possibility-manned bombers are going to play a smaller and smaller part and have a lesser degree of impact. Almost everything I read suggests that the only threat would be from
I.C.B.M.'s. That being the case, why does the government continue its present policy? Why does the Minister of National Defence outline in his white paper the policies that are outlined about the expenditures of money by the Canadian taxpayer for his department on something that is utterly useless in the event of war? From all I have read they are still a long way from getting a defence against the I.C.B.M.; but even if the United States is successful in the breakthrough, it is a matter that involves billions of dollars, not only in the breakthrough but in setting up the defensive apparatus. This is something completely out of the field of operation of Canada in any way whatsoever now or in the future. Is there not a better way in which Canadian money could be spent on peace, rather than spending it on our Bomarcs and Voodoos? Is there not an explanation due, not only with regard to present expenditures but also past expenditures? Many of us are still waiting and are intrigued to find out why it was that the former government bought the planes we now have for our squadrons in France and Germany. I understand that we were the only country which bought them to be equipped with nuclear warheads. Now that the CF-104's are in France we have to put in the dual system.
Not long ago I asked a question as to what was the cost of making the change-over, but I could not get this information from the associate minister. Who is paying for this? Who is responsible for the stupidity of ordering planes to be equipped in this fashion, in view of the policy of the French government at that time? Yes, Mr. Speaker, I am looking at the Conservatives, who knew about it at that time. I think the house should have been told about this.
The important matter now is what the policy of this government is today. In my estimation the white paper does not disclose basic, fundamental, futuristic government defence policy. The government is still living in the world of the past, perhaps a little

bit of the present, but not at all of the future. That is why it is interesting to us at this time to note that since the last election we have not heard any more of the previous Liberal policy, and more particularly the policy of the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson). Under his interpretation of that policy the government had a commitment to fulfil, because of past Conservative policy; but he promised to renegotiate the Canadian position with regard to nuclear warheads. The Minister of National Defence shakes his head. Does the Minister of National Defence deny that that was the statement and the challenge that was made in the last election by the Liberal party and the Prime Minister? It was broadcast across Canada that there would be such a renegotiation, and that it was his desire to negotiate Canada out of the nuclear business. I have not read or heard of any move by the Prime Minister or the Minister of National Defence to renegotiate themselves out of the nuclear business or to renegotiate our position in NATO. I cannot remember seeing or hearing anything to that effect.
I understand from the press that when the defence committee filed its report at the end of the last session there was only one major point on which the minister disagreed with the committee, and that concerned our brigade in Europe and the Honest John nuclear rocket. I have seen no explanation yet of the minister's disagreement on that point. No statement has been made by the minister as to exactly what is the position of our brigade in Europe. Is it a mobile brigade with conventional weapons and high mobility, or is it to be concentrated around poor Honest John? The Minister of National Defence must know that the tactics of conventional warfare are concentration and mobility. The tactics of nuclear warfare are those of dispersal. Yet our brigade in Europe is concentrated around Honest John, which the defence committee had an opportunity of seeing last fall.
Surely Canada is not going to take the initiative in starting a nuclear war. Therefore, in a conventional war we are concentrating on Honest John, which of course would not be used. If an enemy were to start a nuclear war, then instead of the tactic of dispersal we have the tactic of concentration. These are some of the questions which we think should have been answered by this time.
Quite apart from our brigade in Europe, our squadrons in France and the position Canada is now taking with regard to NATO, with what could lead to a breakup, there is also the question of our naval policy. I have not heard one word yet about our naval policy, except with regard to the building of three
National Defence Act
submarines. Just what the three submarines are going to do, I do not know. These are some of the matters about which I think we should have heard. I doubt whether we will hear about them for a long time, because this will most likely be the last opportunity for some time to have a discussion in the house on defence matters. We can only express the hope that when the committee meets, and meets three months or at the least two months late, there can be the fullest possible information made available, that witnesses and experts will be called and that the Minister of National Defence and the Associate Minister of National Defence will have time to sit in on the deliberations of the committee-because I do not see how these matters can be discussed unless we know the government's views and policies, and are told how they reached their decisions.
At risk of repeating some of the matters which might have been raised on Friday, I should like to close my remarks by expressing my disappointment that our defence committee has lost two months of opportunity. I regret very much that we have not heard more of the fundamental and future policy of the government, especially with regard to what I consider, and what I think the people of Canada consider, the commitment made by the government to get out of the nuclear role. Because it has no place for Canada at all.
The place for Canada is that outlined by our party years ago, and I am mighty glad to see that the Prime Minister is now moving towards it, namely that of a United Nations peace force. There again, sir, I am disappointed. For the past three years two Scandinavian countries have been working on this matter and have reached the point where their legislation is ready. I was very happy to read in the press that the Prime Minister is going to invite countries to a conference to discuss this matter. But we, Mr. Speaker, should have been in the lead, and we would have been in the lead had this government and the previous one listened to the good advice it received from this party in years past.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I did not intend to take part in the debate this afternoon-I know that most members want to see the defence committee set up as soon as possible-but, during the debate, I heard several comments to which I should like to reply, and I must say that the points brought up were rather disappointing. I was particularly surprised at the stand taken by my colleagues, especially the hon. member for Pon-tiac-Temiscamingue (Mr. Martineau) and the hon. member for Joliette-L'Assomption-Mont-calm (Mr. Pigeon), when they dealt with the royal commission on bilingualism and bicul-turalism in relation to the armed forces. It is a fact established by custom and tradition that members of the armed forces do not take part in debates on public or political matters. As a matter of fact, there was only in the house-

speechtext: May I put a question in order to clear up the matter? Is it not rather a question of prohibiting members of the armed forces from taking part in discussions on political matters?

No, Mr. Speaker. Under the regulations, members of the armed forces are prohibited from taking part in public discussions on controversial matters. Besides, in the house itself, some members of the armed forces were rather strongly criticized for having expressed their personal opinion at a certain time of their career on controversial public matters.
When the royal commission on bilingualism decided to investigate in the Department of National Defence, we saw fit to maintain this tradition, while allowing members of the armed forces to appear before the Lauren-deau-Dunton commission, but behind closed doors. Certain persons seem to think that members of the armed forces are being denied a right and that they are considered as second class citizens. I do not see it that way. In my opinion, they are granted a privilege in being able to give evidence in that manner. Many members of the armed forces are given the opportunity to appear freely before a royal commission, secure from any reprisals; they can thus state exactly their problems, as regards bilingualism and biculturalism, in the Department of National Defence. The Laurendeau-Dunton commission will thus be in a position to hear members of the armed forces on this important subject.
Now, I think that it would be absolutely illogical and premature to conduct another investigation as it has been suggested. I think that the Laurendeau-Dunton commission


should necessarily be given the opportunity to hear all representations on bilingualism within the Department of National Defence.
My hon. friend from Joliette-L'Assomption-Montcalm referred, a while ago, to what he had read in a newspaper. I am not ready to confirm or accept the newspaper report according to which Mr. Lauziere freely suggested that discrimination existed within the armed forces, and even if he said it, I would not dare justify nor set up a new inquiry into that question of discrimination. If there is any, it certainly did not start this year, it must date back to some time already. The Laurendeau-Dunton commission is making a serious effort, and so is the government, to study the question of bilingualism not only in the country but also within the Department of National Defence. We in the department want to help as much as possible our members to testify freely; we want to give the Laurendeau-Dunton commission all the information and help it needs to reach the proper conclusions.

I would like to direct only one question to the minister; after that, I shall ask him no more questions.
Since the royal commission on bilingualism and biculturalism only plays a passive role- it hears only grievances-and the government does not have to implement its recommendations-that commission may sit for one or two years-and in view of the serious charges made, could the minister, in the public interest, ask the officials of the Department of National Defence to conduct an inquiry in order to verify the accuracy of those statements?

Mr. Speaker, it seems to me that I have been explaining that for the last few minutes. It is true, as stated by the hon. member, that the government does not have to implement the recommendations of the royal commission. I can say this, however. The government fully intends to see that there is no discrimination within the armed forces or the Department of National Defence. Still, I do not feel it is necessary to carry out another investigation, which would be premature and might prejudice the work of the Laurendeau-Dunton commission.
I should like to point out to my hon. friend that what we are trying to do within the Department of National Defence, has not been done for a long time and is a conscientious effort. We want all Canadians, both English speaking and French speaking, to be treated equally. I admit that there may be certain difficulties within the department but it would not necessarily be intentional discrimination. It may be, for instance, that French Canadian servicemen, because they do not feel quite at

home in an English environment or community, cannot be fully efficient. There may be problems of that nature, and we evidently have the intention of getting to the core of the matter so as to correct the situation.

I should like to direct a last question to the minister. According to statistics, a mere 2 per cent of high-ranking navy, air force or army officers, who earn $7,000 or more, are French Canadians.
Could the minister say whether that is due to the French Canadians themselves or whether that can be explained by other factors?
For instance, m view of General Allard's competence, could he not hold rank higher than or at least equal to General Walsh?

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING REPLACEMENT OF CHIEFS OF STAFF COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, these questions are exactly those which are to be studied by the Laurendeau-Dunton commission. That is why I maintain that it is useless to carry an investigation within an investigation. This is precisely the point.
Now my hon. friend speaks of General Allard and General Walsh. There is also General Bernatchez. My hon. friend has only mentioned two French Canadian generals but there are others. Even if I do not have the particulars before me, I am convinced that the percentage of French Canadians with senior ranks is much higher than the 2 per cent mentioned by my hon. friend. I think that it is exactly the type of question which will be looked into by the Laurendeau-Dunton commission. Therefore, I see no point in our carrying out another investigation.
The hon. member for Joliette-L'Assomption-Montcalm (Mr. Pigeon) mentioned the establishment of a four year course at the St. Johns Royal Military College. I must say it is not the first time he or I speak of that. It is true that the hon. member for St. Jean-Iberville-Napierville is particularly anxious to have a four year course set up at that institution. Indeed, many other members are also interested in that question.
Moreover, I told my hon. friend some time ago that a thorough study is being carried out in that connection following representations made by the Knights of Columbus, and various other people and organizations. A rather thorough study is being conducted within the Department of National Defence. I was given to understand that this study should be completed in about ten days.
There would no doubt be certain advantages in extending to four years the course given at the St. Johns Royal Military College. However, there are also some disadvantages. According to the experience I was able to acquire in the past year, I feel that the present system involves a decided advantage,
National Defence Act
since it allows our future officers to get acquainted with their English speaking colleagues so as to get to know each other much better, because after all, those young men will be called upon to work together in the future.
Under the present system, after two years at St. Johns Royal Military College, junior officers are sent to Kingston where they meet their colleagues from other parts of the country. At that time, a state of mind is created which I feel is most useful. Besides, I went personally to the Royal Military College at Kingston where I spoke to young cadet officers who had come there from the military college at St. Johns. I noticed then that they were absolutely delighted to acquire that new experience.
As a matter of fact, I think that it is quite normal, because these young cadet officers during their career might come in contact with one another, and it is important that this may start as soon as possible during their military training. It is a great advantage to be able to exchange cadet officers between military colleges.
Now, as I said to my hon. friend, a report will be submitted very shortly as to whether or not there should be a full four year course at the military college at St. Johns.

Some question has been raised about the militia, and the reasons why we did not wait for the defence committee to sit before making decisions with regard to the militia. As hon. members know, the department had arranged a certain schedule and under that schedule it was decided that we should try to arrive at a reorganized militia in which the numbers would be somewhere around 30,000. It was after taking that decision that the Suttie commission was instituted, and I can report to the house that the results of the Suttie commission's efforts so far have been most gratifying. They have been able to travel throughout the length and breadth of the country to all areas where militia units have been established. They have made a very thorough and complete study of the problems involved in the militia and, according to schedule, I understand they are to bring down a report by the middle or end of June.

omy, the question of budgeting and the requirements that will be needed, and it is on this basis that the number was established. subtopic: GRAND CANAL-INQUIRY AS TO ENGINEERING AND ECONOMIC FEASIBILITIES
GRAND CANAL-INQUIRY AS TO ENGINEERING AND ECONOMIC FEASIBILITIES
speechtext:
That, in the opinion of this house, the government should give consideration to the undertaking of adequate and complete studies to determine the engineering and economic feasibilities of the grand canal proposal and to initiating such negotiations as may be necessary with the provinces of Ontario and Quebec and with the government of the United States to ensure their fullest co-operation in this project and that in particular the government consider:
(1)	The problems concerned with the regulation and conservation of the water levels, water flow and water quality on the great lakes, the St.

Lawrence river, the Ottawa river, lake Nipissing and the French river which are a matter of increasingly serious and frequently expressed international, national and provincial concern, particularly with regard to the prevailing low water levels on the great lakes and on the Ottawa river, making as one result only the practical extension of new navigation facilities on the Ottawa difficult to accomplish.
(2)	The hazards to some of these waters created by increasing industrialization and the resulting increasing demands for withdrawals and consumptive use, particularly on the great lakes-St. Lawrence system.
(3)	The effect upon the standard of living of the many and increasing millions of people involved in one way or another with the above bodies of water and the corrective measures of a positive nature that can be undertaken.
(4)	The proposal that certain substantial and renewable sources of fresh water be collected by cross channels on the James bay watershed and then be diverted southward by the Ottawa and great lakes by step-pumping developed in economic stages as needs increased making use of the large potential of unharnessed hydro power in that area.
(5)	Ways and means to facilitate the early construction of the Ottawa river seaway.
(6)	Ways and means to derive the largest possible benefits of a long term nature that may result from the implementation of the Grand canal proposal, such benefits including the revenue from the sale of water to those who would withdraw or consumptively use it, revenue from new hydro power development for the proposed Canadian power grid, new opportunities for northern forest development, new low cost navigation facilities from Montreal to James bay.
He said: Mr. Speaker, the motion now before us has been moved for the purpose of requesting and, in fact, imploring the government to take the necessary action at this time to alleviate a serious and continually deteriorating situation. I have spoken about the low level of water in our great reservoirs of fresh water, the great lakes, and perhaps to a lesser extent in the St. Lawrence river system. The present motion asks for three things. I have been turning them over in my mind and I cannot see one valid reason why the government should hesitate a single second to accept the motion.
One of the things I am asking is that the government initiate a feasibility survey on a project known as the diversion project. The second request is that the government institute talks and consultations with the other governments concerned. I must say, Mr. Speaker, that once again the federal government has abdicated its responsibility in a matter which is crucial to the Canadian people. These consultations are so urgently needed that it has taken another jurisdiction, the government of Ontario, to initiate action that the federal government has failed to take.
I am asking for consultations first of all with the jurisdictions that are masters of the resource in question, the provinces of Ontario and Quebec, and for consultations with the

United States government, whose country is vitally interested in this question.
Finally, the motion asks that the whole matter of water levels on the great lakes, and one project in particular, be referred to the international joint commission. These are simple enough requests. The need is apparent enough, and the negligence of the government has been too apparent. This is an appeal to the government to study the problem of water-water required for increased consumption by the increasing millions of people who are directly interested, living on the shores of the great lakes and within a radius of some hundreds of miles of those bodies of water.
It is also an appeal to the government to show its interest in the development of our natural resources, in the development of cheap, abundant, hydroelectric power which is necessary for expanding our industrial society, and which is also necessary to service the pumping stations that are envisaged by the program the motion outlines. Finally, it is an appeal to the government to look into the existing needs in Canada for more navigable routes to make cheap methods of transportation available to the government and the people of Canada, which would come from an intelligent interest on the part of the government and then action, if action is warranted, to put this plan into execution. I may add that it is also an appeal to the government to aid northern development by favouring the project which is the subject of my motion.
The era of inexhaustible water supplies is fast fading. When I was thinking today of the low water levels on the great lakes I was reminded of the story which I read not very long ago concerning a situation which had developed on the Missouri river in the United States. It is a story told by Mark Twain, the story of an old riverboat captain navigating down the Missouri when the water levels were very low and he was being continually trapped in the sand. At one stage of his journey he saw an old cabin on the side of the river, and someone was outside it dipping water out of the river for his own private uses. The captain excitedly yelled to him, "Put that drop of water back into the river. We need it to navigate." The situation has not reached that stage yet, but the story illustrates in a practical way what the need is and what the need will be as time goes on.
I cannot accept the theory of the minister of northern affairs (Mr. Laing) who has said, "Well, why worry about low water levels today when perhaps next year the levels will be much higher"? Over the long term the story has been one of fast fading water resources, because of mismanagement in the
Water Resources
past and of the present tremendously increasing consumption of water. We shall never again live in an era when we will have too much water, and it behoves us to share it on an acceptable basis with others who perhaps have a greater need of it.
President Eisenhower made a statement with respect to water supplies in 1955, and if it was true then it is much truer today. He said:
If we are to continue to advance agriculturally and industrially, we must make the best use of every drop of water which falls on our soil or can be extracted from the oceans.
Even by 1955 those who had studied the situation saw we would have to convert water into a manageable resource. Today the situation has become more dramatic. Day after day the government is asked to provide some relief, but all it can say is, "Let us pray for rain." That kind of statement denotes a sorry lack of planning, and the absence of a serious approach to a serious situation.
But if the government has done nothing about this situation, fortunately others have. In the forefront of those who have given some study to the problem I would place Mr. Thomas Kierans of Sudbury, who has engineered and fathered a very comprehensive plan known as the Grand canal proposition which, to the minds of more and more informed people, is becoming a practical way of solving the chronic problem of low water levels on the great lakes and providing many other benefits as well.
I have in front of me a model, prepared by Mr. Kierans, showing an outline of the Grand canal proposal, and I may explain that the word "Grand" is an abbreviation of the words "great replenishment and northern development" canal. This is the project which I am asking the government to consider. Some people may say that it is an utopian project and cannot be accomplished in our day.
Even if that were so-and I think I can prove it is not so-the essence of government is, surely, planning and the administration should at least not refuse to consider the proposal. They say it is utopian. But what alternative method is there of providing a benefit which is indispensible to millions of people. In the United States, consideration has been given to the project. We have read of the request made by Senator Hart that the government of the United States should institute talks on this subject-a request which brought out in a dramatic way the great need that exists. Only last week the government of the province of Ontario took action in this regard and increasingly this project is coming to the fore. It has been described as a challenging and an imaginative plan. Moreover, I can add, it

Water Resources
is a realistic one. Yet the government throws up its hands and assumes that what we are facing today is an act of God with which we cannot interfere. This has been made clear many times by the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources (Mr. Laing) as well as by the Minister of Industry (Mr. Drury) who admitted that at the joint ministerial meeting held recently no constructive proposal was put forward to deal with this problem.
I should like in the few minutes which remain to me to outline some of the elements of the plan. First, the need for replenishment concerns not only the great lakes but the Ottawa river system and the St. Lawrence river system. This plan envisages making available new run-off water from a suitable portion of the James bay watershed. It is a multiple purpose plan, controllable and expandable, providing a substantial new inflow of water. Depending how far it is completed, it can provide an inflow into the great lakes of between 4,000 and 75,000 cubic feet of water per second. If we consider the benefits which derive from the plan, the cost is relatively modest and from an engineering point of view it has already been accepted by experts in the fields of engineering, hydroelectric development, navigation and so on. Rigid specifications provide long term benefits for large sections of northern Ontario and Quebec. The plan would also provide cheap hydro power by means of a reversible pumped water storage reservoir system. The specification also includes provision for a new, positive international and interstate joint policy in order to manage the level, flow and quality of the water entering the great lakes. It provides for new inflows from the James bay watershed. It provides for a self-liquidating project as a result of payments made by those who will most benefit from the diversion. It means stepped-up development in northern Ontario and Quebec. It means recovered water, not head water run-off-in other words, the water resource affected is one which today serves no useful purpose and which is unlikely to serve any useful purpose in the foreseeable future. The route follows the shortest and lowest elevation to the great lakes, with low cost cut-throughs throughout.
With regard to the administrative authority to be set up-and this is important, because we know that the resource itself comes under provincial jurisdiction-the establishment of an international authority between Canada and the United States is envisaged, as well as a federal-provincial authority including Quebec and Ontario. It has already been stated that the feasibility of the project is

established from an engineering point of view. From an economic viewpoint, the cost, as I have mentioned, is not likely to be excessive in relation to the benefits brought about as a result of the increased availability of water. Part of the cost will be recovered out of revenues resulting from increased hydroelectric power. A further element of the cost will be recovered from royalty payments by those using the water. Finally, revenue will accrue from the new navigational possibilities which are envisaged. Further-and this is one of the most attractive features of the whole plan-it provides an effective and plausible means of making the Ottawa river a navigable stream open to deep sea shipping throughout its entire length. I say this because the increased flow of water will raise the level of the Ottawa river to a point at which the amount of dredging and canal work necessary to make the river navigational would be greatly decreased.
These are some of the reasons why I urge the government to give this project the consideration I believe it deserves. I should like, if I may, to table with the consent of the house the specifications which relate to it. These specifications contain an outline of the proposal and a map showing where the diversion will actually take place, traversing as it does the Abitibi region, the Harricanaw, the Timiskaming region, the whole of the Ottawa river system, lake Nipissing, the Mattawa river, French river and, finally, Georgian bay. It also includes definite engineering specifications with regard to some of the problems of a physical nature which are created by the project. Second, the cost of the project is dealt with and, third, the benefits to be obtained are outlined.
I should like to table these documents, the outline and specifications of the Grand canal proposal, as an exhibit. I think the government can still redeem itself. It is not too late. It is never too late. It can redeem itself by accepting this motion and getting busy- by getting its officials to study this plan and meet with those who have already given it the best of their thought and energy, thereby evolving a long term project which would provide immense benefit to all Canadians, particularly those who live in eastern Canada, including northern Ontario and Quebec, and to residents of the Ottawa valley who have for generations been asking that something be done with this majestic river which flows through the very heart of the capital and which now remains unused.
