subtopic: GRAND CANAL-INQUIRY AS TO ENGINEERING AND ECONOMIC FEASIBILITIES
speechtext:
I am intrigued by the motion put forward by the hon. member for Pontiac-Temiscamingue (Mr. Martineau). One of the questions which appeared shortly after the Christmas recess in my name was question No. 20, which asked:
What studies have been conducted of the proposals authored by Thomas W. Kierans and O.K.H. Kierans for a great replenishment and northern development canal?
As appears on page 512 of Hansard of March 4, 1964, the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources (Mr. Laing) gave this answer:
This proposal, often referred to as the grand canal, was described by Mr. T. W. Kierans before the standing committee on mines, forests and waters on 11 April, 1960. While no detailed studies were undertaken, preliminary examination indicated that it was physically possible but not now economically feasible.
As the water resources of each province are administered by and belong to that province, subject to certain federal responsibilities, e.g. regarding international waters, fisheries and navigation, any feasibility study of a diversion scheme such as this should be undertaken in co-operation with the provinces concerned.
This answer is general in its nature. I have been interested in this subject because of the constituency which I represent, and I was able to obtain certain further information.
Hon. members will remember I have had questions on the order paper such as the one which was answered on April 15, 1964, question No. 623, relating to water levels in lake Ontario and specifically asking the government what have been the causes of the present low water level of lake Ontario. This is a matter of some concern to anybody living in the Thousand islands area. Indeed, we speak of the city where I reside as the Thousand islands city, and I have heard it suggested by some of the people-

subtopic: GRAND CANAL-INQUIRY AS TO ENGINEERING AND ECONOMIC FEASIBILITIES
speechtext: Where is that?

subtopic: GRAND CANAL-INQUIRY AS TO ENGINEERING AND ECONOMIC FEASIBILITIES
speechtext:
The city of Brockville. The concern of some of the residents, in the sense of their interest in the water, is that if water levels continue to decline as has been experienced this past year, we might be the city of three thousand islands. This is a real possibility, because we have many
Water Resources
shoals and rocks throughout this St. Lawrence system which, of course, could seriously impede navigation.
I have a personal interest in water levels. I live in a house that is a good deal older than 100 years, and the eight of us in our house are serviced by a well. It might interest hon. members to know that the principal well driller, Ralph Miller of Hallecks, told me that 100-foot wells are no longer adequate now and that there is a fear that many existing wells may have , to be constructed 60 feet deeper because of a sharply lowering water table. This year we have had a poor year because we did not have snow and we have not had sufficient rain. I have observed in my own farm pond, which is stocked with bullheads, that the water level at the present time is about two feet lower than it was a year ago. A series of articles have been published in the principal newspaper in our area regarding this question. The Recorder and Times of March 25, 1964 describes the situation in these words:
Water levels of the St. Lawrence river are at their lowest ebb in 30 years and the situation is causing concern to municipal officials from Iroquois to Gananoque, as well as to shoreline residents whose boathouses and docks are being affected.
When we look at the over-all picture, the
situation is becoming rather serious. We have docks that are now many feet above normal position. We have seen a drop in water level of four feet to six feet, and in some areas it has been even more than this. Prescott has been complaining for three weeks of dirty water in the town water supplies; this was on March 25. The situation has been drawn to my attention by Thomas C. Cossitt in letters, and a series of letters have been written to our press; and then, commencing in the month of April we see there has been a steady improvement. The Recorder and Times of April 6 tells us:
Fears had been expressed that navigation might be hindered by the low water now prevailing in the St. Lawrence system. Water levels up and down the stream are two to four feet below normal, but seaway experts said the usual April rains now due should do much to alleviate the situation.
We have not yet had enough rain, but we find the low water problem is substantially easing. In regard to this motion, Mr. Speaker,
I point out that there has been a good deal of debate recently on the subject of water. This is helpful and it is an emphasis that certainly, as a representative of Leeds, I am very happy to see. On the south my riding is bounded by the St. Lawrence river in the area between Kingston and Prescott, and on the north it is bounded by the Rideau system.
I have had the opportunity on two occasions to navigate in my boat the Rideau canal from Kingston to Ottawa, Ottawa to Montreal and

Water Resources
on to Beauharnois and back again, so I am familiar with the points raised by the hon. member for Pontiac-Temiscamingue when he referred to particular navigation problems as they relate to the Ottawa river.
I think there is a good deal of logic and sense in what was said by the parliamentary secretary to the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources (Mr. Turner) when he spoke on May 4, as reported at page 2912 of Hansard. He said:
-given the engineering feasibility, at any point in time, any kind of engineering solution can become economically practicable-
I know, sir, that when I first travelled the Rideau I was amazed at what Colonel By had done 150 years or so ago with respect to these waters. He was able to provide navigation from the Ottawa river to the St. Lawrence river. More particularly, when you ascend or descend the magnificent Carillon locks on the Ottawa you appreciate what really can be done by modern engineering. In the standing committee on external affairs we have had the chance to listen to experts talking about the relative merits of power sites such as Mica, Downie, Luxor, Bull river, Dorr, and we see whether it is in Montana, Washington or British Columbia we can do almost anything we set our minds to do, in an engineering way. Almost anything can be done; the real test is, does it make sense at a particular time? Of course, in determining this we have to recognize this other fact, that no great scheme, engineering or economic, can possibly come to fruition unless there has been a great deal of research and thoughtful consideration given to it long years in advance.
I take considerable satisfaction in the fact that the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources on May 5 said that he intends to refer the whole matter of water levels to the standing committee on mines, forests and waters. I ask hon. members of the house to consider whether the hon. member's motion is not too specific in its content. After all, what he is asking us to do is follow six specific recommendations. I think we should have been happier had these recommendations been much more general in character. In particular, he would have the water flowing into the Ottawa river in preference to Georgian bay.
When we look at this gigantic scheme we realize how many different considerations are involved. I must say I have been very much impressed by the presentations of Mr. Tom Kierans and the conversations I have had with him. I think he has made a real impression on any hon. member who has taken the trouble to acquaint himself with the James bay diversion scheme.

Mr. Speaker, I should like hon. members to have some idea of the chronology of these Kierans presentations to the government. I ask the hon. member to note that on January 25, 1960, Mr. Tom Kierans of Sudbury outlined to the then minister of northern affairs and national resources a proposal for the transfer of James bay water to the great lakes via the Harricanaw, Ottawa and French rivers.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, could I ask the hon. member a question?

subtopic: GRAND CANAL-INQUIRY AS TO ENGINEERING AND ECONOMIC FEASIBILITIES
speechtext: Certainly.

subtopic: GRAND CANAL-INQUIRY AS TO ENGINEERING AND ECONOMIC FEASIBILITIES
speechtext: If this project has already been referred to and studied by the committee on mines, forests and waters, why does the hon. member now propose that it be studied again?

subtopic: GRAND CANAL-INQUIRY AS TO ENGINEERING AND ECONOMIC FEASIBILITIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would indicate that the proposal put forward to the preceding government in the correspondence was given cursory consideration by the government of the day, of which the hon. member had the honour to be a minister and apparently the scheme presented by Mr. Kierans was considered to be physically possible but economically unpractical. This is the answer given by the hon. member's own government to the specific proposal presented. They said that James bay water must be lifted more than 1,100 feet vertically to enter the Ottawa river headwaters. I am not going to go into detail, Mr. Speaker, because there are other hon. members who would like to participate in this debate, but second, they pointed out that:
Imported water must he virtually free of salines.
Imported water is water which would be used for consumptive purposes elsewhere.
This would require salinity reduction equipment or construction of barrier dams in James bay to create freshwater areas. Any barrier dam near the Moose river outlet must incorporate navigation locks for entry to the port of Moosonee.
Then they came to the third conclusion, that
___the Harricanaw river lies almost entirely within Quebec, which would have to give its consent to such proposed use.
We have had recent experience with another province to appreciate how jealous it can be of its primary jurisdiction over national resources. Then they determined, fourth, that:
Additional storage may be required to avoid waste of diverted water under high natural great lakes inflow conditions.
They came to the conclusion that:
Sale of water to the United States is unlikely to be continuousas I believe was envisaged in the proposal by Mr. Kierans-

-particularly during cycles of high natural inflow.
Then, sixth, they came to the conclusion that:
Navigation benefits are limited by the short open season on James bay and in Hudson strait.
Then they decided that:
A diversion of 25,000 cubic feet per second would increase present lake Ontario inflow only by perhaps 12 per cent-
-and that this 12 per cent figure would not appear to be adequate to improve materially pollution conditions which have been existing at Toronto for some time. Then finally the Conservative government of the day came to the conclusion that-
-any water sold to the United States would not be available for use on lakes Erie and Ontario and on the Niagara and St. Lawrence rivers.
These were the conclusions respecting the first proposal. Subsequently, Mr. Speaker, the same Mr. Kierans, under date of March 21, 1960, submitted an amended plan which proposed the collection of the water from the several rivers and its transportation to the Harricanaw river by a series of dams and canals, rather than the use of James bay water for diversion. That proposal was studied, and I will not take up the time of the house with it because any hon. member can acquaint himself with the conclusions arrived at by the former government. However, I must say that notwithstanding these adverse conclusions I have much sympathy for the general ideas set out in this project and I think it is absolutely necessary that we now start to think carefully in this general direction.
I am sorry that the hon. member has brought before this house a motion so specific and detailed that it is almost impossible for many of us to agree with it. If not-

I find it difficult to understand for example why the fourth proposal, that certain substantial and renewable sources of fresh water be collected by cross channels on the James bay watershed and then be diverted southward by the Ottawa and great lakes by step-pumping developed in economic stages as needs increased, making use of the large potential of unharnessed hydro power in that area, is made with specific preference to the Geor-gion bay route.

subtopic: GRAND CANAL-INQUIRY AS TO ENGINEERING AND ECONOMIC FEASIBILITIES
speechtext: First of all, Mr. Speaker, let me say that I cannot presume to speak for the government; I am simply giving a few views of my own.

subtopic: GRAND CANAL-INQUIRY AS TO ENGINEERING AND ECONOMIC FEASIBILITIES
speechtext: Give us your own opinion then.

subtopic: GRAND CANAL-INQUIRY AS TO ENGINEERING AND ECONOMIC FEASIBILITIES
speechtext:
I do not want to prevent other people from contributing to the debate, but even after the extensive debate which we have had on the subject of water in recent days I am pleased that the hon. member has had the foresight to bring this resource problem to the attention of the house. I am glad we are focusing attention on what these two Kierans brothers have been thinking and worrying about these many years.
I care a great deal about this matter, Mr. Speaker, because it seems to me that we have a tremendous resource in our system of waters. As we listen in the standing committee on external affairs, to the tremendous projects which are envisaged for the west coast, I think we have to think again about the grand canal. This is inevitably going to come to pass in time. I do not fully comprehend the exact recommendations contained in the motion of the hon. member nor do I know precisely what is desirable, but the government must certainly apply its mind to the problem. In this regard I rejoice in the fact that the minister of northern affairs has had the courage and the wisdom to send this to the committee for study. I hope this is only the beginning, because from what I can discover the examination by the former government has been rather casual.
I think it would be selfish towards other members, Mr. Speaker, to continue my remarks for long. This amazing recommendation takes a watershed away from its original course to James bay and redirects it to the great lakes and it really matters little whether it goes into Georgian bay via lake Nipissing and the French river or whether, as is now suggested, it goes into the Ottawa river, because these are mere details. The scheme- and it is a gigantic one-is to change the course of a mighty watershed.
In this regard I was impressed by an editorial by Richard J. Needham which comments upon a statement made by the minister of northern affairs in the house a few days ago, to the effect that we had better pray for rain. That is not such a silly suggestion as one may think. I was reminded

Water Resources
by the brilliant dialogue between God and Job, which is to be found in the thirty eighth chapter. God speaks down from the heavens and says to Job:
Where wast thou when I laid the foundations of the earth?...Or who shut up the sea with doors, when it brake forth...
and here shall thy proud waves to stayed?
And further on, not viewing a reply, God said to Job:
Hast thou entered into the treasures of the snow? or hast thou seen the treasures of the hail,
Which I have reserved against the time of trouble-
Even in my county of Leeds this spring we have discovered that we need snow as well as a good deal of frost and rain, and the people in my part of the country are praying for water because we feel no one else can raise the level of the waters.

subtopic: GRAND CANAL-INQUIRY AS TO ENGINEERING AND ECONOMIC FEASIBILITIES
speechtext: I should like to pray for the government.

subtopic: GRAND CANAL-INQUIRY AS TO ENGINEERING AND ECONOMIC FEASIBILITIES
speechtext:
The minister of northern affairs apparently believes in the efficacy of prayer. Then God said to Job:
Who hath divided a watercourse for the overflowing of waters...or a way for the lightning of thunder: [DOT] [DOT] *
-Who can number the clouds in wisdom? or who can stay the bottles of heaven-
The likelihood is that we are going to be doing generally what has been outlined by the hon. member, if not right away then certainly before very long. We have to do it. It is perfectly clear that we cannot simply hold for ourselves the rich resources of water. After all, it cannot be regarded on a local or even a national basis; broader considerations arise. In a sense it is a case of making ourselves partners of the Creator himself, and the changing of a watershed is an exciting challenge which I think lies ahead.
We all have much sympathy for the proposition that the government of Canada has now to think in terms of broad, bold schemes. There are great difficulties in the Kierans plan. What are we going to do about salt water? If that problem is solved, then what are we going to do about navigation? Certainly the cost at the moment is prohibitive judging from every government study undertaken heretofore, but as the parliamentary secretary indicated what is prohibitive now may not be prohibitive two or perhaps 20 years from now. I hope that the government will be stimulated and encouraged in this matter by the committee to which this question will be referred, thus providing the necessary impetus to sound and enlightened policy with respect to our rich resource of water.

subtopic: GRAND CANAL-INQUIRY AS TO ENGINEERING AND ECONOMIC FEASIBILITIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we support this motion. It is very easy to cavil and make the kind of petty qualifications made by the hon. member for Leeds (Mr. Matheson), but I do not think that in this sense the detail is significant in relation to the wonderful scope of the plan. We seem to need physically big projects in Canada to capture the imagination. I can think of the South Saskatchewan dam, the Passamaquoddy project and the Chignecto project, the latter two still being in the visionary stage. The St. Lawrence seaway certainly aroused support, agitation and irritation for almost a century before it was brought to completion. The disappointment with the results of the St. Lawrence seaway, I suggest, should not make us hesitate about finding out more about this great scheme of Mr. Kierans'. I have had the pleasure of listening to Mr. Kierans and talking to him in Ottawa, as I recall some time when the former government was in power. I remember meeting him in a committee room. It is not fair to say that this is a bold, new idea. It is a bold idea, but he has been pushing it very strongly and getting increasing support.
Some of the questions I should like to ask about this project really do not relate so much to the details of the motion. The last part of the motion indicates great navigational possibilities, particularly in the Ottawa river. This has never appealed to me as much as the idea of the waterpower to come. In my own riding there is a diversion, for example, from the Hudson bay watershed into the great lakes watershed. I refer to the Ogoki diversion, which attracted me. I have tried to find out if there were any drawbacks to the Ogoki diversion. The difficulty is that there are few people living up in that area. The Indians to whom I have talked really have had no complaints. The fringe of civilization and exploitation has not really moved much over that watershed, in so far as the lake Superior littoral is concerned. It is not quite the same when you get into Cochrane, Timmins and Tim-iskaming areas. Even there, it seems to me we need to think a bit about what will be the final consequences of the program when it is finally achieved in terms of the effect on the watershed itself. Surely, there will be consequences for the Hudson bay littoral.
When you get a distance-the distance changes-from 150 to 300 miles north of the actual height of land from the great lakes into the Hudson bay system, you begin to run out of forested areas that are worth while. Any member who has flown over the James bay-Hudson bay regions knows that as you get towards the coast you fly over a

low, swamp, muskeg-kind of spruceland. One thing I should like to know in connection with this scheme, if it has an effect upon the actual amount of water available, is whether there is any possibility-this may be a century ahead-of resurrecting or converting some of the muskeg land by means of drainage into something that will be more productive.
If I go over to the lake side of the watershed, I find we are talking about water tables. How much are the water tables down because of bad conservation practices, bad forestry practices? We have denuded so much of the land and have done so little about putting the land back into forest cover. This is something we do not know, but it seems to me it is tied into the motion presented by the hon. member and it is quite relevant. One of the things of which we do not have a picture at the moment, although it comes out very strongly and particularly from the Chicago area, is the need for water to handle pollution possibilities. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, during the course of this debate and during the question period today reference was made to the special benefits that the government is contemplating paying to servicemen who are to be retired before reaching the normal retirement age, and I thought perhaps it might be useful to say a few words on that subject this evening.
As hon. members will recall, in the process of integrating the armed forces it is estimated that we would have to cut back the number of servicemen by about 10,000, and we estimate that it would be possible to effect this reduction in a period of two years.
In order to do this most effectively and to achieve the objective that we have set ourselves in national defence, it is contemplated that this retirement should be made compulsory and through selection. I would like to make it quite clear to the house that this is in no way any reflection whatever on the personnel who are to be retired. On the contrary, all of the people who will eventually be retired compulsorily are people who have served the services with devotion and loyalty for many years, and it would be wrong for the house or the country to read into these releases any other meaning than that which is true, and that is that it is in order to reorganize our national defence.
The reason for the release of such a large number is because there will no longer be employment under the new career structure of a reorganized national defence for the people who are being released. It is because of the good services that have been rendered by these people, and because the government fully appreciates the difficulties these servicemen will encounter in trying to readjust to civilian occupation, and in order to help them to rehabilitate themselves in civilian life, that the government has decided to pay them a special cash benefit, which would be paid in one lump sum.
This special cash benefit is of course in addition to any normal leave that may have been accumulated and, as hon. members know, this leave is paid in the form of cash. It is also in addition to the pension to which a serviceman would normally be entitled, and in addition to any transportation benefits which he would normally receive.

National Defence Act
It is important to realize that the special benefit envisaged here is not applicable to people who are released for misconduct, or inefficiency, nor would it be made available to people who want voluntarily to leave the service. It was suggested during the course of the debate that what we should do is pay this special benefit to those who would willingly and voluntarily leave the service, but I do not think I have to expand very much on the reasons why this is not being done. There are obvious reasons, but the main one is that what we are trying to do is to select the people we feel will be necessary within the services, and also select those who unfortunately will no longer have employment under the reorganized department.
As hon. members know, this special cash benefit will increase with the length of service, up to a maximum of the equivalent of 10 months pay for those with 15J and more years of service, and it will be reduced progressively as normal retirement age is approached. I believe hon. members will realize the reason for this. Someone who is about a year from the normal retirement age would already have some idea of what he is going to do once he is retired. His plans are firmer than those of the man who is about five years from retirement age, and it is for this reason that the special benefit is progressively reduced as normal retirement age is approached.
Further, as hon. members know, this cash benefit is subject to income tax. During the question period this afternoon a question was asked as to whether representations were made by the servicemen with reference to the imposition of income tax on this benefit. I have not had any official representations by the servicemen in this respect, but I, like other hon. members, have seen the reports in the press and it is not impossible that the press is reflecting the thinking of the servicemen. However, it might be useful to remind the house that this cash benefit is indeed a revenue and, according to our principles of taxation, it is taxable. Another point is that the serviceman, if he had remained in the service until his retirement age, would have been obliged to pay the full tax on the amount of money he would have received. Under these arrangements the tax is calculated on the basis of 85 per cent of the tax rate established by reference to normal service income. So a man compulsorily retired will pay a lower tax rate for the benefit than he would have paid had he stayed in the services.
I appreciate this is a delicate problem. The Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) in the answer he gave this afternoon said the matter would

be looked into and that the suggestion having to do with staging payments over a period of time would also be examined. I presume a statement will be made on this subject in due course. Included in the plan, there is also as hon. members know, the waiving of the present provision in the Canadian Forces Superannuation Act which provides for a 5 per cent reduction in annuities for those servicemen who have less than 20 years of service but more than 10, with a maximum of 30 per cent. This penalty was imposed on servicemen in order to encourage them to stay in the services until their normal retirement age was attained and it was felt by the department that it would be most unfair to continue the penalty in circumstances where a man was compulsorily retired. The other provision in the benefit plan is that an unreduced gratuity would be paid to officers holding short service commissions. This is, in essence, what is contemplated.
We have seen in the papers some references to the special benefit plan being as a kind of "golden bowler". There are not many references of that kind. Others started calling it a silver stetson, and recently these particular benefits have been described as a straw hat. I rather like to think of this benefit plan as being just an ordinary fedora. While it is more substantial than a straw hat it is less spectacular than a golden bowler. It is adequate and it does only what it is meant to do, that is, to try to help servicemen who will be compulsorily retired rehabilitate themselves in civilian life.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, now that the minister has been kind enough to answer all the questions put to him, I should like to take part in the debate and make a few remarks.
First of all, I should like to congratulate the minister on the positive aspect of his aim in military matters. Having said this, I must warn him that my further remarks will not necessarily be flattering, because unfortunately, I found in his white paper some negative points that I shall attempt to denounce in a few minutes.
With regard to the military policy he intends to apply in Canada, the minister, in his white paper, stated his intention to carry out several recommendations submitted by the defence committee in its report tabled a few days before the end of the session last year, that is in December 1963.
The integration of armed forces under a single command seems to have been the main concern of the department. That decision is probably the one which has received up to now and will receive the greatest support from all hon. members, even if a few have expressed certain doubts as to the timing of this integration.
I think that most of us agree that this integration of armed forces is essential. I also think that this integration is supported by
[Mr. Winch.)
most Canadians and more especially by the members of the armed forces concerned.
It is evident that this development was essential to avoid a waste of manpower and of the huge sums required for the administration of the national defence.
One of the main reasons for integrating the armed forces is to prevent military leaders from exerting too great an influence on the minister who must answer to the country for the phenomenal amounts voted each year for that purpose.
I do not think such integration creates a precedent since recently, England, which is often quoted here as an example to follow, has broken with century old traditions to bring all the armed forces under the authority of a single minister. Mr. Speaker, efficiency dictated such action.
It would seem that, left to themselves, the military have or at least had, with the best intentions in the world, the tendency to build up an empire and try to impose their views on the various governments which follow each other at the head of the country.
It is therefore urgent, in the light of developments, that civil authorities regain control of expenses this government has to make or justify before the Canadian people.
Bill No. C-90 suggests the establishment of a chief of the defence staff position. I believe that, after this bill is passed by the house, the man entrusted with this responsibility will have a very important part to play in the future of Canadian military forces.
It is therefore most necessary that he should submit to general instructions to be given to him by the government through the minister who, for his part, is held responsible to the people by the bill he submits every year at the time of the budget.
Mr. Speaker, the integration of armed forces will not occur without any trouble. Some people's toes will have to be trod on and we must expect, from some parts of the country, criticism against this measure. However, I believe that it is necessary for us Canadians to support this measure, which was moved almost unanimously by the house and has the support of a great majority of Canadians.
In the past, and especially since the end of the war, the forces have had perhaps somewhat exaggerated appropriations of public funds. I believe that when the minister decided, as proposed in the white paper, to freeze for a few years the expenses of the military budget, he definitely took a step in the direction intended by the majority among us, and I think he will necessarily have to go further.

The minister claims that such a decision will bring a reduction in the budget generally voted for the country's defence. Of course, such a reduction will be in proportion to the development which will take place in the other sectors; it will amount to almost $1.5 billion, but it will not be a reduction on present expenditures. A study of the budget shows that the Canadian people will not benefit by a reduction in the amount of taxes levied during the year, because the estimated expenditures will be the same for that military defence, or rather that so-called defence, since, after all, being realistic, all of us in this house, must vote a more than reasonable portion of the national budget for a defence against aggressors that seem to be rather hypothetical.
I think, Mr. Speaker, that if we really wish to come back to reality, we will have to reduce further the percentage of the amounts appropriated annually for national defence. In fact, if we analyse the amounts spent annually by countries similar to our own in the world, we realize that most of them, even the members of NATO, that alliance to which we belong, spend an amount representing some 8 per cent of the national budget. Now, if we consider that, in our case, the amount provided represents some 25 per cent, that is one quarter of the national budget, it is clear that we have much to do before we come closer to the standards now used by other countries that do not have the ambition to pass themselves off as something they are not.
I think that at present the Canadian people have to pay a bill imposed on them by governments which did not take into account the fact that Canada has a population of only 19 million, and that accordingly it could not afford to spend more than it was justified to, in a field which is not necessarily related to progress or to the Canadian economy.
The integration of the armed forces is apparently something which will mean a saving for the country, but unfortunately, it will bring about a reduction of our military personnel.
When the minister announced last fall that he might close certain radar stations, certain army or air force bases, certain radar bases in the north, some hon. members protested that decision which affected them personally in their riding.
I was thus able to realize to what extent we, in Canada, just like the people of the United States, but in a larger proportion, had an economy based on military industries. If we consider all the reductions now being made in the various governments
National Defence Act
throughout the world, we see that all sensible people are worried about the present trend to disarmament. People wonder what will happen when we stop looking after the needs of the thousands of men now in the forces, which contributed to the employment of thousands of industrial workers who produced their equipment.
We are led to ask on what basis exactly we have built our economy.
When we think of the war years 1939-45, we realize that we, in Canada, did build up an industrial economy resting on the needs created by a war waged on the European continent. When, from 1939 to 1945, we used part of our potential in the construction field for destructive purposes, we failed to consider that after that war we would have to build up and erect a system which would enable us to live and create a peacetime economy.
When we refer to the figures prevailing in post-war period, we realize that until 1950, the annual amount voted by the government to cover military expenditures was more or less the same until 1950-52.
At the time, expenditures in the defence budget stood at around $350 million annually. Suddenly, due to certain fears, we deemed it advisable to increase that amount to $1.5 billion from 1955 on. And each year, almost without fail, we made the mistake of voting that sum of $1.5, because we had to make an impression, through such an expenditure which was way beyond our means, and play a role which did not suit us on the international scene. I do not think anybody was impressed.
We were thereby proving to other countries which were older than we were that, to a certain extent, we were irresponsible in the circumstances since we were mortgaging the future of a country which has such a tremendous need of its credit, its potential.
When we consider Canada's share in the cost of international organizations, we realize that the part we play is always out of proportion to our capabilities. We have tremendous potentialities, but they are still undeveloped. They will remain so for some time to come, probably for decades. I feel, therefore, that it would be wise at this time to determine our position and to ask ourselves what amount we Canadians should reasonably appropriate for those peace keeping operations in which our role is very minor. Up to now Canada has never been called upon to decide whether or not there would be a war.
The only part it has played was to decide whether it would participate or not. Unfortunately too often, certain authorities have

National Defence Act
decided that we would participate without previously asking the agreement of Canadians to bear the expenses.
Mr. Speaker, if we consider what is going on at the international level, we realize that within the framework of NATO, for example, now holding a conference of ministers from which Canada is practically absent, the voice of our country therein is not predominant, we have tried once again to play a part which was not ours. Let us compare Canada with its 19 million inhabitants with France which has 50 million and Germany which has 60 million. If we realize, on the other hand, that we are more than 3,000 miles away from that military field, we must honestly admit that our part in the circumstances is extremely limited.
This afternoon the hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Winch) criticized the attitude of France and of its president, General de Gaulle, towards NATO, especially France's decision to withdraw temporarily its support to NATO. Mr. Speaker, I feel that to blame France in that specific case is a mistake because we Canadians are hardly in a position to judge the circumstances which prevail at the present time on the European continent. We must recognize that Europe has been rebuilt, that it is powerful and that it wants to play its own role, without being controlled or directed by another power located about
1,000	miles from its territory, a power we all know, the United States. We must admit that, up until now, NATO has been the tool or instrument of the United States and that only the Americans have been able to impose their views concerning the decisions and the action taken. If France now intends to assert itself and to speak out against decisions which, to a certain degree, are taken unilaterally by the United States, she has the right to do so, and we would be ill-advised to criticize the position she has decided to take.
I believe that NATO's role in future years will be just as important as it was in the past but it will be determined by the countries concerned, that is Belgium, France, Germany, Italy and the neighbouring countries, in accordance with their military needs.
Everybody admits that the military situation is changing. Mr. Speaker, we must admit it and, as I suggested to the minister this afternoon, we should take advantage of this opportunity to renegotiate immediately, even before it expires, the agreement we signed, so that after 1966 we will be able to make changes in this field, as we ought to, that is our role will be symbolical and psychological rather than practical. I mean that if we admit that the CF-104 squadron, for instance, which is now based in Europe, will be outmoded within

five years, we will have to admit that, after that date, Canada will not have much to say in this field and will have to submit to the decisions taken by the authorities of those countries directly concerned by the European military problem.
Mr. Speaker, I should now like to deal with another problem, Cyprus. I shall have a few questions to raise, especially the part played by Canada in the U.N. force. We decided, probably with a certain haste due to circumstances, to send a military force to try and maintain peace on the island where there is now a kind of civil war. I feel that as a French Canadian, I have a few questions to ask. I did not do it at the time that decision was taken, because I did not want that point to be questioned. But I wonder now why it was decided that it would be a group of French speaking Canadians that would try and maintain peace on Cyprus when the majority of French Canadians are accused of being incompetent to hold high positions in industry and the federal civil service. How is it that it was deemed advisable to send French Canadians to Cyprus to try and maintain peace on that island which was under British control for perhaps centuries, an island where the languages usually spoken are Greek, Turkish and English and where practically not a single word of French is spoken. How is it that French Canadians of the 22nd regiment were selected?
Please note, Mr. Speaker and Mr. Minister of National Defence, that I am not against it. On the contrary I am proud, to a certain extent, of the fact that French Canadians were asked to carry out a task that was recognized by everyone in this house as a very delicate one. But since it was admitted that French Canadians could play a delicate and difficult part in a land utterly unknown to them, how is it then that there are in Canada Canadians who refuse to acknowledge the fact that French Canadians can actually contribute to the building and development of this Canada of ours?
And at this stage I should like to call earnestly for an acknowledgement of the part played by the French Canadian group in this Canadian force. I am against those who want Quebec to secede from confederation because I feel that French Canadians are able to play a role not only on Cyprus island but also in Canada, not only in Quebec but also in Vancouver and in Halifax.
I think we have a right to aspire to play that role. We have the competent men required. It was recognized that we had competent men in the military field, and I think that some day Canadians, whatever part of the country they come from, will have to

agree that we also have the right and the capability to fully assume that role in every field.
Having said that Mr. Speaker, I feel that, as Canadians, we must accept that all Canadians, from Halifax to Vancouver, be treated on an equal footing so that wherever they carry on their activities they may benefit from all the advantages they are entitled to. As a matter of fact, since we have proved that we were able to play a part on the Dieppe beaches, the Normandy coast and even on the island of Cyprus, I believe that we have the right to demand that we be allowed to play our part in any sphere of activity, be it economic, social, political or cultural, on our own soil.
Reference was made this afternoon to the special defence committee. That committee was set up last year and it was my privilege to be one of its members. However, like the hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Winch), I deplore the fact that it was not set up again sooner during the present session.
Certain circumstances have probably prevented the leader of the house or the Minister of National Defence from bringing forward that project, but I feel the house has thereby lost a certain opportunity, because during the last two months we could have examined more thoroughly the government's defence policy and especially the white paper tabled by the minister.
Furthermore, we could probably have made an even more useful contribution to the present debate, because, personally, I have no feeling of animosity towards the previous administration or the present government. They did what they considered to be the right thing; they are doing what they think is the proper thing to do now, and I am of the opinion that time alone will tell whether they were right or not.
There is one very special case I should like to bring to the attention of the house tonight. It concerns certain soldiers who will be discharged soon or who have already been discharged. As a matter of fact, I have already submitted some of those cases to the Associate Minister of National Defence, and that has made me wonder about the efficiency of the training and technological courses being given in our military camps.
The case of certain servicemen who returned to civilian life after five years of service was called to my attention. After exerting their efforts in a particular field in which they had acquired a practical and technological experience, after leaving the army, navy or air force, they were deprived of the right to use their knowledge in civilian life,
National Defence Act
because the military training they had received did not meet the requirements of the various departments throughout the country. Besides, the minister is well aware of what I am talking about, because I told him recently about the problem of young men who had left the navy after five years of service. They had worked as electricians, operators of boilers and stationary engineers, they had obtained some certificates attesting that they were qualified to practise their trade. But after their discharge, they were not even accepted as apprentices in their trade. After having spent five years to learn a certain trade, these young people could not, after their discharge, exercise the trade which they had learned while they were in the navy or other divisions of the Canadian armed forces.
Mr. Speaker, I believe that there is a certain anomaly which the Department of National Defence should undertake to correct immediately, in order that those young people may take advantage of their knowledge acquired during their service on their return to civilian life. In fact, when these young people complete their military service, they should be able to obtain evidence of the skills they have acquired which will allow them to practise the trade they learned, exactly as their fellow citizens practise a trade or a profession in civilian life.
When we invite our young people to join the navy, the army or the air force, we lure them with all the benefits involved in acquiring technical knowledge which will be useful to them later on. Now, I believe that if we wish this propaganda, this publicity to be true to reality, arrangements should be made with the provincial authorities in order that knowledge and skills acquired be recognized by the various departments, so that these Canadian citizens may honourably earn their living, when they are pensioned off or when they end their service in the Canadian forces.
Mr. Speaker, evidently, I may be wrong, but I am of the opinion that the special committee on defence did last year a very good job, and I think we can admit, without bias, that the group forming the committee which was established last Friday will also proceed in the same direction.
Of course, this committee should study several areas, but I believe that in the light of the study made last year, a very particular point on which its members should dwell is the economic repercussions which disarmament may have in future, since we today recognize it as a need.
Disarmament is advocated by many organizations, by several groups, economic, social as

National Defence Act
well as political, and I believe that the committee should pay a great deal of attention to the economic results of future disarmament on the Canadian economy in particular. May this disarmament come as soon as possible.
The committee should thoroughly consider this matter in order to submit definite recommendations to the government so that it may establish the necessary machinery which would prevent disarmament from becoming the source of economic changes which would create a crisis such as the one we knew in the thirties.
If you study the statistics published by the United States, you come to the conclusion that Canadians will just have to consider that particular point. As a matter of fact, I read recently a report on that subject and I must tell you that it is disquieting to note that the American experts cannot see at the present time what solutions could prevent disarmament from plunging the country in economic chaos, which would probably push the United States, and certainly Canada, indirectly, in a crisis which surely nobody wants.
Mr. Speaker, Canada is spending huge sums for national defence. Sometimes, in our constituencies, people are asking for what purpose exactly such sums are spent. When people are giving us sound arguments, we find it very difficult to justify the spending of a billion and a half figuring in the national defence budget.
As a very influential person put it, not only should we consider the possibility of "freezing" the national defence budget at its present amount, but we should even consider reducing it and use the money thus saved in a more profitable field.
We want to spend a billion and a half to defend ourselves against a hypothetical enemy. Mr. Speaker, I am sure that the Canadian people would welcome the spending of part of that money in the field of national health, where a true danger exists, where we are threatened by two enemies, cancer and heart disease.
When we consider the amounts allocated every year to research and case-finding in connection with these two illnesses, we come to the conclusion that we have lost completely the sense of responsibilities and values.
I think that if we apportioned a larger amount to research, to the detecting of those two plagues, and to methods of fighting them, the Canadian people would readily agree to pay the taxes required to pay for research in those two areas because it would bring a

solution to a problem which is not hypothetical but really factual, since recently, a colleague of ours was struck down by one of those two diseases.
I think that in that field, Canada could make a much more valuable contribution which would be readily accepted by everybody since it would be valuable, not only for Canada, but also for all nations in the world which could benefit from it.
Mr. Speaker, I do not wish to prolong this debate, but I think that when the committee on defence resumes its discussions on military problems in Canada, it should necessarily take into consideration those two points I just mentioned and some others which may have been pointed out by previous speakers.
I feel sure that if we give careful consideration to those matters, we will while playing a part in the military field, do our share to safeguard peace, because it is in that direction that we should channel our efforts.

maintopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING REPLACEMENT OF CHIEFS OF STAFF COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, before proceeding with what I had in mind to say tonight, I should like to make a few comments on what the Associate Minister of National Defence (Mr. Cardin) said here some half hour or more ago. To begin with, I should like to say I have no objection to the gold bowler concept, as it is called in the United Kingdom, of giving a certain amount of lump sum compensation to servicemen retired before their normal time of retirement arrives. However, I think two mistakes are being made in regard to this, and I would like to put them before the two ministers for consideration.
In the first place it is grossly unfair to charge income tax on these lump sum payments. The minister mentioned something tonight about some amelioration so far as that is concerned, but I honestly believe income tax should not at all be charged on these lump sum payments. The fact that they are lump sum payments connotes that they are paid to people to compensate them for the lack of leave and pension they would have earned if they had gone on to their normal retirement time.
If the two ministers have undue difficulty with their colleague in the finance department and in the treasury board, I would suggest that the very least that could be done would be to spread these lump sum payments over three or four years so far as income tax purposes are concerned, so that the income tax would not be assessed all in one year, or even two years.

The other point I would like to make in connection with this is that from my experience in the Department of National Defence I found there were always a considerable number of people who wished to retire before their time was up because opportunities had presented themselves in civilian life. I believe there is a considerable number of people in the armed forces in that situation at the present time, and I think they should be allowed to retire and be given the same pension benefits as though they were compulsorily retired. In this way the department would find it unnecessary to retire as many people compulsorily as otherwise would be the case, and also the general morale of the armed services and of the personnel in them would be considerably better than if the plan which is proposed is carried through.
I know, of course, that quite often people in the services who want to retire are people who the authorities consider are occupying key positions, and that it would impair the efficiency of the services if they were let out. But we must always remember that nobody is indispensable in the armed services, just as this applies anywhere else. I believe these people who are prepared to leave voluntarily at present, even though it is thought they are occupying key positions which it would be difficult to fill, should be let go. This would ease the situation considerably and produce better results than the plan that is evidently in prospect.
To address myself to the bill which is under consideration, Mr. Speaker, my remarks on it will be relatively brief, for the very good reason that the bill provides really only one thing, and that is the legal basis on which unification of command in the armed services can take place. It provides for the abolition of the positions of chief of staff of each of the services, and the substitution of a defence chief of staff for the present three individual chiefs.
I believe that the minister's remarks in this debate on Friday, together with the white paper which he previously issued, confused two quite different things, namely unification of command and integration of the armed services. The point was made by the hon. member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert) on Friday-and I think it needs to be reiterated and emphasized-that these are two quite different things; but the minister's speech and the white paper tend to blend and confuse them, and thus make for confusion in the minds of the general public and of members of this house.
There are probably very few students of military affairs at present who will not agree that in war, at least, unification of command is desirable if not essential. The reason for
National Defence Act
this is that in the future most military operations are likely to be of a combined character, in other words, an army-air force operation, an army-navy operation, a navy-air force operation, or an operation involving all three services. This being the situation there is no question but that unification of command is something which should be put into effect.
Actually this was started several years ago right here in the Canadian services. For several years now we have had a unified naval-air force command on the Atlantic coast, and a similar one on the Pacific coast-the maritime command-in which the admiral in each case was the maritime commander of that coast and the air force officer was his deputy commander, and they operated a combined force of ships and aircraft. Undoubtedly this is the pattern of the future. This is the sort of thing which we are going to have more and more of, and I do not think anybody can seriously quarrel with or complain about the proposition of unified command. It is chiefly a matter of whether or not it is put into operation effectively.
However, Mr. Speaker, I would like to make the point that unification of command does not necessarily mean integration of the services. These are two quite different things. The United Kingdom and various other countries have instituted unification of their commands, but they have not instituted integration of their services. I hope that in his future statements with regard to this matter, perhaps in his remarks when he closes the debate, the minister will make it clear that these are two different things, not try to give the impression he did at the very beginning of his remarks on Friday that this change which is proposed-and I read from Hansard at page 3065-
-is the first and perhaps the most important move in the integration of the armed forces under a single defence staff.
That statement may be correct but it gives rise to a wrong impression and it tends to confuse people's minds on this subject.
As to integration itself, I think the chief difficulty is that we have had no hard information with regard to the integration of the armed forces on the basis of which we could determine what is being planned, or come to any reasonable judgment with regard to the matter. We have not been told what the word means. The word "integration" has been used to a considerable extent by the minister and it appears in the white paper but its meaning has not been defined, and what the hon. gentleman intends to do with regard to integration has not even been hinted at so far. At the present time, then, we are debating this particular matter in a vacuum. I think this vacuum should be filled as soon as possible

National Defence Act
in order that we may have an actual idea of where we are going as far as the integration of the services is concerned.
No doubt integration of the armed forces of the navy, the army and the air force can and should take place. It has been going on, in fact, to a certain extent for a number of years. I presume what the minister has in mind is a considerable speeding up of a process which has been in effect in certain areas for a long time. For example, the dental needs of the three armed forces have always been met by the Canadian army dental corps. The medical services and the chaplain services were integrated several years ago. The pay scales of the three services were put on the same basis some time ago; the supply of food to all three services has been looked after by the Royal Canadian Army Service Corps. These are all examples of what has taken place already in the field of integration of armed service administration. I should like to sound a word of warning in connection with this matter. I think considerable care needs to be exercised to ensure that what has always been the objective, as far as the integration of armed service administration is concerned, is met. The integration of the medical services and the integration of the chaplain services did not meet our expectations in this regard. In other words we did not secure the savings in manpower and, thus, the general savings, which it was hoped these moves would bring about. However, I do not think there is any doubt but that the integration of these administrative functions is highly desirable. It ought to be put into effect and it should be put into effect as rapidly as possible.
However, I am afraid, from what I have seen in newspapers and from my impressions of conversations with members of the general public, that most people in Canada have an idea that integration of the services means that all servicemen will be in one vast organization-that they will all wear the same uniform, that they will all be interchangeable and that the whole military organization as we have known it will disappear. This idea is, of course, a highly erroneous one. It is not practicable and it is not possible. Individual units in our armed services at the present time are highly specialized. If we are to have an effective military organization, they must remain so. It is impossible, for example, to move an artillery officer to the command of a destroyer or to move an army service corps officer and make him the flying officer of a transport plane. All the units which exist at the present time in the army, the air force and the navy will, in effect, have to continue being the same type of units as they are at the present time. This is something
[Mr. HarknessJ
that should be made clear to the general public. I have run into this idea time after time, talking to people in casual conversations as I go about this country. This idea, as the minister I know recognizes, is not a practical one, and the sooner the general public can forget this impression of what integration may mean, the better.
I really have nothing else I wish to say in regard to the bill under consideration but I should like to make a few comments in connection with the white paper. The white paper put out just before Easter deals chiefly with broad generalities. It ends by saying, on page 30:
In this paper no attempt has been made to set down hard and fast rules for future policy and development. Flexibility, not rigidity, has been the keynote. The paper is a charter, a guide, not a detailed and final blueprint. The policy outlined in it is not immutable. It can be altered or adapted to meet the requirements of changing circumstances, national and international.
I think it was very wise of the minister to put in that broad escape clause. But the point I want to make is that this white paper, regardless of the escape clause, raises far more questions than it answers. It deals, as I said, with broad generalizations and it gives us none of the definite information we need in order to exercise sound judgment on the plans the government has in mind. In fact it does not disclose what the policy is to be. It is so broad in its approach that it really does not mean very much at all. I am sorry to have to say this, but I think it can be characterized largely as what might be called a publicity stunt designed to present a good image of the minister and of the government to the Canadian people. Rather than being a real white paper giving us clear answers with regard to defence policy it is simply a piece of publicity. The first half of the white paper, approximately the first 15 pages, deals with the objectives of defence policy and the historical development of policy since 1945, together with an exposition of the international situation which determines the threat we may have to meet. I defy anyone in this house or in this country to find anything in those 15 pages that I did not say myself during the period when I was minister of defence or that my predecessor General Pearkes did not say. Those 15 pages are a straight restatement of what one might call the basic facts of defence, as they have been recognized by everybody who has had to deal with them or study them during the last ten or 15 years.

speechtext:
I am not at this time, because I have not time to do it, going into the broad questions of defence policy which are by and large dealt with in the first 15 pages of this report. However, there are a few things in the last 15 pages of the report particularly on which I would like to comment briefly. For this purpose I will take the sheet which the minister issued with the report and which is called "Highlights, white paper, 1964". I have not too much time, Mr. Speaker, so I will deal with this very briefly. The first thing mentioned here is the ten year plan, and then in brackets it says "First such long term defence plan". I defy anybody in this house to go through that white paper and see any reference to a ten year defence plan. It is just not there; there is no ten year defence plan, and there is not even a ten year defence plan mentioned in the white paper. Nevertheless the minister puts this out for the use of the newspaper people, of course. The first item on it is, as I have said, "Ten year plan (first such long term defence plan)". If the minister has a ten year defence plan, let him give it to the House of Commons; let him give it to the country. We have not heard of any ten year defence plan; we do not know of any single item in it. As a matter of fact, this is one of my chief criticisms. The minister has done a lot of things of which I approve and with which I agree, but one of my chief criticisms is the sort of business along this line. He tries to sell this like a ten-ring circus and gives a totally false impression to the people of Canada in regard to defence measures, which in my opinion are much too serious to be dealt with in that way.
The next is flexibility, and the next is mobility. If the minister will go back and read the speeches I and my predecessor made in this house time after time, to say nothing of those made throughout the country, he will see that flexibility and mobility have been stressed year after year after year. It has been the objective of defence policy and 20220-200$
National Defence Act
the objective of equipment policies to give the greatest degree of mobility and flexibility to our armed forces.
The minister mentions integration and the unification of our forces. I have dealt with that. The next is "Deputy minister's powers increased". This, if course, has reference to the Glassco commission report. I think some of the recommendations of the Glassco commission in this regard are extremely sound, and the sooner they are put into effect perhaps the more effective and efficient will be the Department of National Defence. I have no quarrel with that item. The next thing we see here is "Management system for defence programming to be introduced". If we look at page 20 of the white paper we see the following statement in this regard:
It is intended to introduce into the Department of National Defence a management system for planning and controlling major defence programs at the departmental level. This system will display various components of the long term defence program in suitable detail over a significant time period. The system will provide a means of expressing various force structures, weapons systems, logistic arrangements and other military activities in terms of their immediate and long term costs.
I have read that paragraph at least a dozen times now. I have had many years of experience in regard to these military matters, and it does not mean a thing to me. It is the greatest gobbledegook I have ever read. I think it is a disgrace that nonsense of that sort should be put into a white paper and presented to people as though it were a reasonable thing. If anybody in this chamber can get any real sense out of that paragraph, I would like to see them and I would like to have them explain it to me, because I think I have had perhaps as much experience as anybody here in regard to these things, and that paragraph just means nothing and is nonsense of the worst kind.
I would hope that in future statements and future white papers the minister would be wise enough to eschew things along that line, a bunch of words that means nothing and which it is hoped will impress the uninitiated; and perhaps it does, but certainly anybody who knows anything about the subject will look at it and the sort of expletive that will come to one's mind is not that which can be used in this chamber.
The next thing I see here is "Many Glassco commission recommendations to be implemented". That is fine, but which are they? We do not know which are to be implemented and which are not. The white paper does not tell us, and the minister has never told us, which of the Glassco recommendations as far as defence is concerned are going to be put into effect. That is the sort of hard information we should be given here, instead of

National Defence Act
these broad general statements which do not mean anything. The next is "Future air squadrons to be in direct support of ground forces". What is that, except a pious hope, Mr. Speaker? I think anybody would subscribe to the fact that this would be desirable, but in the white paper or in anything the minister has said at any time there is absolutely nothing to back this up as to when it might happen, if it will happen, and so on. It is just a statement such as saying, "I am against sin". Everybody agrees with that, but what does it mean?
Next is "Air truck fleet being extended; sea lift being augmented". If the air truck fleet is being extended, this is a highly desirable move and I commend the minister and the government for it. I understand from the newspapers they have given orders for another 12, I think it is, Hercules air transports. We bought four of them several years ago for the purpose of experimenting with them, evaluating them and seeing what use they would be. They proved extremely successful. Of course, the idea was that the number of these Hercules aircraft would be increased if We found them satisfactory, and I am glad this is being done. I would hope that more Caribou aircraft would also be purchased along that line.
Now we have the sea lift being augmented. Looking back into this matter it seems that what the minister has in mind is to buy some of what we might call cargo vessels or the equipment in order to carry army personnel from point A to point B, or something along this line. I would hope this would receive a very careful second look and going over, because I think it would be a complete waste of money. You can, as the first and second world wars demonstrated, always hire civilian sea transport for transportation purposes, and for us to spend defence dollars on ships which would be very, very costly in comparison with ordinary cargo ships, in order to have the capability of lifting a certain number of personnel by sea from one point to another would, I think, be a very, very bad waste of defence dollars and I hope nothing along that line will be done.
The next thing here is "A study under way to determine best, cost-effective anti-submarine equipment for future". That is fine. Studies are always good; I have nothing against studies. But a study is no substitute for ships actually in being or under construction. This is the only thing the minister has to substitute for the frigate program which he destroyed and for the ships which he has taken out of commission or has sold as scrap or put into mothballs. All he has to substitute for all these ships which have now disappeared, and the future ones which

will not be delivered to the navy when it was planned that they would be delivered, is just a study of the program. As I said, that is not good enough. The actual effectiveness of the navy has been severely cut down and their future effectiveness, as far as we know at the present time, is going to be almost destroyed in the course of time because no program for the rebuilding of ships has been put into effect or is even far enough along so that the minister can make a promise about it, let alone anything else. They are a few of the matters in the white paper, although I do not wish to comment on them at this time.
I should like to end by saying that my chief criticism of the minister and the government from the defence point of view is that the defence capability of this country is being steadily reduced. Nothing is definitely going ahead to replace the equipment which is being laid up or taken out of commission. What this amounts to is really a unilateral decision on our part to reduce the contribution which we had agreed to make to the north Atlantic alliance, and is also a diminution of our ability to meet any commitments which the United Nations may make upon us. This is my main criticism as far as defence is concerned. The minister has been knocking off this, slashing away at that, decommissioning something else, and putting nothing in their place except a lot of big promises. After a year in office it is now time for big promises to come to an end and for the minister to tell us definitely that certain things are going to be done, and to state our program and policy. To date we have had nothing except promises.
