speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in listening to the hon. member for Calgary North (Mr. Harkness) it was quite apparent that he was dealing with specifics. It is not my intention this evening to do that. However, before actually launching into what I have to say, may I say that I should like to congratulate the hon. member for Lake St. John (Mr. Lessard) on the constructive aspects of his speech, but the drivel he produced in the middle of it was beneath his dignity as a member, and I found it very difficult to listen to. Surely he does not think that that kind of inflammatory talk will improve relations between the two founding races. Surely he knows that the Royal 22nd regiment was a stand-by battalion and was designated to perform any task such as that of Cyprus which might arise. If it had not been sent on that task I am sure that he, as a French Canadian, would have been one of the first who would have most vociferously objected to the fact that it had been bypassed.

On Friday afternoon, near the beginning of his address, the hon. member for Pontiac-Temiscamingue (Mr. Martineau) said, in essence, that he could see no savings in the suggestion of the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Hellyer), although the minister claims there are. The budget tells us that we spent on defence in the year 1963-64, last year, the enormous sum of $1,699 million. It is true that some economies are shown for the year 196465, and I give the minister full credit for introducing them. But his expenditures in the year 1963-64 were $99 million more than the previous year, 1962-63. This year he will save a bit more than this-actually $109 million. Without intending to be sacrilegious, this seems a case of "the Lord giveth and the Lord taketh away".
In fact, in spite of all the ballyhoo of the minister's white paper, the cuts in defence spending for 1964-65 do little more than return us to the level of Conservative spending. The previous government did its task in keeping defence expenditures down to what I think was a legitimate level, and it was very much misunderstood in some parts of Canada as a consequence of its sensible attitude. It was the Conservative government which, in attempting to keep expenditures to the minimum, cancelled that absurdly expensive scheme for the Avro Arrow plane. That is past history now, but I do not think we should forget it. It was something like a $700 million "lemon"; a plane which we were led to believe could fly for only 15 minutes on its fuel supply and whose cancellation brought to an end the remarkable profitmaking of a firm which had parleyed in a few short years a small investment into assets of many millions, mostly acquired from business done with the taxpayers of this country. If anything needed to be done it was this cancellation; and it was the previous prime minister of this country, the leader of the official opposition (Mr. Diefenbaker), who had the courage to do it.
It was the leader of this party too who had the courage and the good sense to refuse the Bomarcs, those nuclear weapons which are rapidly being outdated and which the military mind wanted, but which I am quite sure the average citizen did not. Let us not be so foolish as to say that there was a commitment to accept them. Surely none of us has so soon forgotten how at Nassau President Kennedy in a few short words cancelled the development program which his country was undertaking for Britain on an air-to-air missile, and forced Britain to take Polaris submarine missiles instead, thus making useless in a minute a plane which had cost her millions of pounds to develop or, if you like,
National Defence Act
tens of millions of dollars. Mr. Kennedy did not hesitate to put his country's national interest first, ahead of a so-called commitment made earlier but which he felt time and changing circumstances had modified and eliminated.
So it is with us. Surely we are not so securely tied to the tail of the American kite, no matter how friendly it flies, that we cannot put our own national interest first. Time and circumstances had changed the Bomarc from a possibly valuable weapon to one which would be useless, a weapon program which the United States secretary of defence, so he said, would not have introduced and would not spend a nickel on, if he had to do it over again. But the Liberal government installed them, and by so doing put us unwillingly into the nuclear club. We did not have to accept them and we should not have accepted them.
This saving is only a small part of what should be done to reduce our national expenditure on defence. We cannot, as other hon. members have said, afford to spend approximately 25 per cent of our total budget on defence when we have deficits of the order of $455 million forecast for the coming year. I should like to quote in this regard from the budget white paper, page 91, under the heading "defence expenditures". It says:
Expenditures of the Department of National Defence and defence expenditures of the Department of Defence Production are again in the largest category of government budgetary expenditure. The total of $1,699 million for 1963-64 is approximately 25 per cent of the aggregate budgetary expenditures of the government for the year and is $99 million more than the total of $1,600 million for 1962-63 when they were 24 per cent of total expenditures.
In a growing and developing country which desperately needs large amounts of capital for use in productive ways, particularly when we have a finance minister who is clearly antagonistic to the use of foreign funds, we cannot divert to useless and non-productive defence expenditures the huge sum of, in round figures, $1,700 million annually.
There is no use saying we cannot reduce our defence budget. It can be done, and it should be done. In addition, it seems to me that much of our present military establishment is based on concepts of how war was fought in the second great war. Even the modifications which the defence minister is proposing seem to be based on the same premise. Such beliefs are as out of date as the Spanish galleon of the great armada when it met Drake's sloops in the English channel or, to use a more modern illustration, as the Maginot line was to the German panzer columns. An imaginative approach to defence

National Defence Act
problems will enable us to phase out much that is no longer vital and concentrate where it seems more worth while.
I believe the minister is trying, but I suggest he has not been imaginative enough. In a couple of years, we should be able to bring our defence expenditures to a more reasonable proportion of our total spending and so eliminate our deficits. This will be possible if, of course, conditions do not change in the world to such a degree as to require more elaborate and expensive defence expenditures, a condition to which we are always subject. Even more important is the fact that by making reductions in our defence spending we will be giving a lead to other and greater nations. We will be adding our little bit to a growing tendency toward disarmament and so to the alleviation of tension in the cold war. It is an appropriate time to take such action.
May I quote from an editorial in the Journal of the United Nations for March-April, 1964 headed "Disarmament has Begun". I quote:
A remarkable thing has happened. After failing, in years of discussion in disarmament conferences, to agree on how to start disarming, the two superpowers have begun to disarm without an agreement. As U Thant has commented, the United States and the Soviet union "seem to have come to the conclusion that no progress towards ending the arms race will be made unless and until they slow down themselves."
Within three weeks of assuming office President Johnson announced that 33 U.S. military bases, seven of them abroad, would be closed down or put on a stand-by basis, and that more cuts were coming. Shortly afterwards, Chairman Khrushchev, announced a reduction in the 1964 Soviet military budget of $600 million. A few weeks after that Johnson cut the new U.S. military budget by $1 billion, and announced a 25 per cent reduction in the production of fissionable materials, with the closing down of four plutonium piles. Earlier, the Soviets had put out feelers to call off, or slacken, the race to the moon.
In this kind of international climate, it seems to me Canada could do her bit to accelerate disarmament. As the months pass it becomes clearer and clearer that the policy of the leader of my party of preparation of the weapon systems for nuclear arms, but refusal of the arms unless or until an emergency arose, was the sensible, intelligent decision. Indeed, it was a decision which would have made it easy for us to give the lead in banning the bomb and leading in and encouraging disarmament. I urge this government, this government with its almost fatal tendency to rush into precipitate action without full consideration of the consequences, to consider this greatest of all ambitions, a peaceful world. I urge them to accelerate economies in defence and to couple these economies with a reorientation of our whole defence policy so that we may once again lead the world towards peace.

should like to enter this debate very briefly, as I am deeply interested in the subject of defence and would like to make one or two observations. First, I wish to congratulate the minister upon the introduction of the resolution to again set up the defence committee. Perhaps I would not be amiss at this particular point if I congratulated the chairman of that committee during the past session, who is now the Minister of Forestry (Mr. Sauve); the vice chairman, the hon. member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert), and also the members of the staff of the House of Commons who served that committee. I feel the committee did an exceptionally fine job, a vital job, during the last session and much is due to these gentlemen.
I dm making one criticism at this point of the setting up of the committee. I feel this move has been made too late in the session. Of course, Mr. Speaker, any committee is only valuable, and can only be valuable, if it is given a job to do. I contrast the committees that we have in this parliament with those in the United States where so much of the work that is done in the congress and in the senate is done by committees. The committee chairmen are considered to be the most important members of the congress and senate. Before I leave last year's committee, I should like to say I feel that not only did it do a valuable job, but it was a credit to the House of Commons.
There were 24 members on this committee who, first of all, had an opportunity of listening to experts in the field of defence. They heard the chiefs of staff for air, navy and army, as well as the chairman of the joint chiefs of staff. They heard some who were experts and some who were not experts. Later, the members of the committee had an opportunity to go to NORAD headquarters at Colorado Springs and to North Bay to see the installations there for the air defence of North America. In addition, committee members had an opportunity of going to Europe to talk to the leaders of Great Britain in the field of defence, including the Hon. Peter Thorneycroft, and the leaders of France, West Germany, Denmark and at supreme headquarters of the allied powers in Europe, as well as NATO headquarters. I feel that the members of that committee came back with an excellent knowledge of the problems of this country in defence, as well as the problems of the whole world in this particular field.
On Friday, Mr. Speaker, I had an opportunity of spending a day in camp Gage-town. This particular military establishment is the largest and finest in the commonwealth. It contains over 420 square miles of training

area and, at its peak in the summer, has
12,000	troops. A new city has been built beside the camp to serve those who are stationed there. I feel that the area commander of New Brunswick and the brigade commander of the camp are to be commended, because they brought in 150 citizens of New Brunswick who watched the training and observed the troops in action. We had an opportunity of seeing field firing by the Royal Canadian Dragoons, the Royal Canadian Horse Artillery and the Black Watch. They are all fine units of Brigadier Wilson-Smith's brigade. We had an opportunity to examine how a camp of this size functions.
In the months of July and August of this year we expect 12,000 troops in that area. I was suggesting to the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Hellyer) earlier, and possibly he thought I was joking, that it would be a good thing if during the summer-if we are in session here, and we quite likely will be-an opportunity could be provided for members of the House of Commons to go to camp Gage-town to watch the Canadian army at its best in its training. Perhaps hon. members would gain some knowledge of how the defence dollar is being used and would come back with an appreciation of this.
Now, Mr. Speaker, the Associate Minister of National Defence (Mr. Cardin) discussed the reduction in the armed forces as a result of this integration policy. This is a subject in which the men and women of the armed forces are deeply interested. I have not had an opportunity of discussing this reduction to any great extent with members of the permanent forces. However, I do know that members of the militia in this country are very unhappy indeed.
We know that a few years ago the previous Conservative administration was bitterly criticized because the role of the militia was changed. It was said that instead of having their machine guns, mortars and other weapons they were given sand buckets and stirrup pumps. What has happened to the militia today is that for the most part they are being almost wiped out. I would tell my personal friend, the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Hellyer), and the associate minister, that the militia of the country are deeply concerned about what is happening to them.
I noticed the other day that the minister mentioned there was a need for more recruits, even with a reduction in the total strength. He said that there was no better career for a young man in this country than to enter the armed forces. That, of course, is very true. One of the roles of the militia has been to be a feeder for the permanent forces.
National Defence Act
It has been in the past and I think it can be again in the future a base for the mobilization of the armed forces if we do find ourselves in another war. Let us hope, of course, that we will never find ourselves in a nuclear war under any circumstances, but if we did the militia could again play its part there.
Recently I put some questions on the order paper directed to the Associate Minister of National Defence (Mr. Cardin). I asked whether he could advise how many civilian employees would be released as a result of integration. The minister gave an answer, which I accepted of course because I thought it was reasonable, that this could not be determined at this particular time. But I would ask the associate minister to give this matter some thought and to see if he cannot allay the fears of the civilians who work for the Department of National Defence. There are a great many men and women, some
40,000	altogether I believe, who are concerned in this particular instance.
We cannot put illustrations on Hansard. I sometimes wonder, though, whether it would not be a good idea. I am going to send to the Minister of National Defence a cartoon done by Chambers. Perhaps he has seen it. It shows a kilted soldier waving his claymore -he is a very rugged fellow indeed-while three others are trying to remove his kilt. Standing to one side is the Minister of National Defence holding a uniform and at the top are the words: "Some things are better left alone, Mr. Hellyer". Perhaps the minister has seen the cartoon, but if he has not I will send it to him. It is one that is really worth framing.
There is a point I should like to bring up. I raised this matter when we were in Europe last fall and I make no apology for raising it at this particular time because I am deeply interested in the dependants of the men who serve in the armed forces-the women and children. I am concerned about the matter of education. We know only too well, of course, that in this country we have 10 systems of education and the children who feel the brunt of this more than any others are the youngsters whose fathers are in the armed forces.
I suggested to Colonel Dick, in Soest last year that it would be a very fine thing for the army to have special classes in the summer months so that the more gifted children could advance more rapidly than by simply remaining in their ordinary grades. I have another suggestion in this regard. I have noticed that at camp Gagetown a high school teacher will have youngsters in his class who have gone to school in half a dozen or more of the provinces. I remember one teacher

National Defence Act
who took only 15 or 20 minutes for lunch and spent the rest of the lunch period working with students who perhaps had never had the subject he was teaching at all-in this case it was French-or had had a very sketchy education in the subject.
Possibly I have not made myself entirely clear but I can explain the matter more fully to the minister personally. I believe that special classes would be an exceptionally fine thing for these students at Soest, Zwei-briicken and other schools overseas in order to help these youngsters who in many cases suffer from the point of view of education because their fathers serve in the armed forces.
There is another matter I should like to raise at this time. It has to do with a rather strange subject known as "Nudets". I put a number of questions on the order paper earlier in the session reading as follows:
1.	Are there any units of the nuclear detection and reporting system-
That is abbreviated to "Nudets"-
__presently being constructed in Canada and, if
so, who is constructing these units and at what locations are they being constructed?
2.	What is the cost...?
3.	What is their purpose?
The answers were:
1.	No units are presently being constructed.
2.	Not applicable.
3.	The Nudet reporting posts are designed to determine the location at ground zero of a nuclear explosion, the height of the burst and approximate yield of the weapon.
Then I asked a second question in these words:
Have any discussions been held with the Pentagon relative to the construction in Canada of units of the nuclear detection and reporting system and, if so, what conclusion was reached as a result of these discussions?
Here was the answer:
Discussions have been held between Canadian and United States officials on matters of mutual concern relating to civil defence on a confidential basis. In consequence, the publication of any results of such discussion would require the consent of both the Canadian and United States governments.
The result was that I was given practically no information at all. So many times when questions are asked on the order paper or on the orders of the day the person asking the question already knows the answer. In this particular case I knew the answer and it does not agree with the one I was given. I wish to quote very briefly from the Saturday Evening Post of December 7, 1963 which contained an article by Stewart Alsop, a highly reputable writer. He said:
As a gentle reminder of the weirdness of the world we live in, and a small warning against excessive complacency it seems worth while having a look at a peculiar product of our times
[Mr. MacRae.l
called Nudets. Nudets is Pentagonese for nuclear detection and reporting system. The Nudets system is being built by the General Electric Company at an estimated cost of $25 million at 52 sites in the United States and southern Canada.
Perhaps the minister can see what I am driving at. Here we are told in one place that they are being built in Canada and in another place we are told that they are not being built in Canada. Perhaps the minister is right but if he is I do not feel it is proper that articles like this should go unchallenged by the Department of National Defence or the Canadian government when we are brought into the picture, if in fact such is not the case.
I have only one very brief point to make before I sit down. This year of 1964 is an anniversary year in many ways for those who have served in Canada's forces in the past. It is 50 years ago that world war I began; it is 25 years since the beginning of world war II, and 100,000 men have given their lives in defence of this country. If it should happen that we should go to war again, let us hope that our forces are completely and fully equipped. War is no longer a feasible or sensible method of settling international disputes.
May I call it ten o'clock, Mr. Speaker?

I regret that the Secretary of State is not in his place this evening. However, I would sincerely hope that the Acting Secretary of

State would be able to give the house some answers with respect to this very important question. It is a very important subject and is of great concern to the civil servants and the members of the armed forces who may be affected.
During a recent visit to northern Manitoba I was contacted by a number of civil servants and some members of the armed forces who complained bitterly about this announcement. Some of these people have been advised that as of October there will be a drastic reduction in their take home pay, in some cases as much as $60 to $95 per month.
Many of these people have been in the area for a year or more, but in some cases less than a year. I believe they went there with the understanding that these allowances could be expected for the duration of their tour of duty. The ones who have been there a year have now gained a considerable experience of working with the people in the area, and are becoming very valuable to their departments. If reconsideration is not given to this policy, then I suppose it becomes a matter that these civil servants, and possibly members of the armed forces, will be entitled to ask for a transfer, just at a time when the money that has been spent on them to date in northern allowances and isolation pay is producing results.
If there had been a significant lowering of the cost of living, a move of this nature could be understood and would probably be justified. With regard to the cost of living I would like to refer very briefly to an article in the Montreal Star of April 9 which says:
Higher clothing, transportation and housing costs helped increase the country's cost of living index from 134.5 to 134.6 in March, the bureau of statistics reported yesterday.

The general question raised by the hon. member is of wide interest and I understand his concern about it. I must say, from the observations he has made, that there is obviously considerable need of explanation, because the point is not well understood. There are some 453 posts involved where isolation, remoteness allowances, are granted in addition to regular pay. The general increase in the cost of living does not have any effect because this is taken care of in the salary adjustments which are made from time to time. We are dealing here with an additional item paid by reason of remoteness. With respect to some of the isolated posts there has been no change at all in the allowance paid. In respect to others, the allowance has been increased, and there are some with respect to which allowances have been reduced. It is obviously those cases where the allowances have been reduced which have been brought to the attention of the hon. member.
The present method of determining isolation and remoteness allowances was developed in 1958 as a result of a survey started in 1956 to correct unsatisfactory situations which had been found to exist under the former regulations. What is being done now is to carry out an adjustment within the regulations on exactly the same basis, using exactly the same tests as applied when they were originally set up in 1958. The points considered to determine the allowances in

Proceedings on Adjournment Motion this elaborate rating system include remoteness, transportation, population, medical services, climatic conditions, entertainment available, schools, the availability of religious services and the provision of water and electricity, as well as the supply of goods available for purchase. These are taken into account in an elaborate point rating system and it is the review of these factors which has brought about a change in the allowances paid. Changes in transportation facilities or, in one or two cases, of telecommunications services and other services have resulted in an alteration in the rates and as a result some posts receive lower allowances -although, as I said, some will receive higher allowances while others will remain at the same level. There is more which could be said but since my time has expired I shall probably have to keep it until another occasion.

Mr. Speaker, last Friday, May 8, as reported in Hansard at page 3059, I sought to put to the Minister of Labour (Mr. Mac-Eachen) this question:
In view of many complaints regarding the onerous application of the availability test for unemployment insurance benefit, has the minister had discussions about this matter with the unemployment insurance commission? Is any relaxation of the application of this test in prospect?
The Chair felt there was not sufficient urgency to this question for me to expect an answer to it on orders of the day. I may say that I do not mind waiting until tonight, but I hope the answer will be a good one. I regret that the Minister of Labour is not here, but if the parliamentary secretary comes up with a good answer, we will give him full marks for it.
I am sure all hon. members of the house are aware of what has happened. Persons who are in receipt of unemployment insurance benefits, and in some cases those who have not yet started to draw them, find themselves called upon to answer certain questions. In particular they are asked what kinds of employment they would take and what rates of pay they would accept. Many of these persons, trying to be helpful, will list certain occupations they would take and certain rates of pay for which they would settle, and a little while later they find they receive a notice from the unemployment insurance commission to the effect that they have restricted their availability for employment and therefore unemployment insurance benefit is either cut off or denied them. That is a simple and direct clarification of what I meant by the
[Mr. McIIraith.)

phrase "onerous application of the availability test for unemployment insurance benefit". It has been drawn to the attention of the government several times during the course of this session, and in the view of many of us who have received complaints from insured workers about this matter, this test should be relaxed. I hope that the answer is a favourable one; that the minister has had discussions about this matter with the unemployment insurance commission, and that we can anticipate a relaxation of this test at an early date.

Mr. Speaker, the hon. member has re-read his question so I think it is unnecessary for me to repeat it. Suffice it to say that up to that moment the minister had not had discussions which would lead to the relaxation of this test as suggested by the hon. member. However, that is not to say that the hon. member's representations will not be considered. But in defence of the officials of the commission I think I should say a few words. The applicable section of the Unemployment Insurance Act, 54(2)(a), provides:
An insured person is disqualified from receiving benefits in respect of every day that he fails to prove that he was capable of and available for work.
The hon. member will note here that the onus of proving availability is on the claimant. In doing so he must show that he is genuinely ready and willing to accept suitable employment immediately; that is, at the time he applies. Also, there must be a reasonable expectancy of obtaining the kind of employment that he is, by his own admission, willing to accept. I am sure my hon. friend does not quarrel with this as an insurance principle.
The hon. member is no doubt aware, also, that there is a wide misconception that unemployment insurance benefits are a matter of right based solely on having established the fact that premiums have been paid. Because of this misconception the commission often finds that a claimant will, in the initial application, indicate that he or she is not interested in obtaining employment. Such person will subsequently change the statement, although having been given a copy of it at the time. It will be on record and the officer must, of course, take cognizance of that fact.
Over the last four years the number of enforcement officers has been appreciably increased, I believe something like 70 in number. The net result has therefore been that a closer check has been made and the administration of the act tightened up. We have no doubt come across a number of people who are really not available for work, and as

a consequence they have been disqualified. If the hon. member has any specific case-

speechtext:
It must be remembered that the Canadian National is a crown company and the minister will not interfere with its

Proceedings on Adjournment Motion administration. However, a report has now come to the minister and the management advises that because of improvements that have been made in recent years to the railroad structure, the railway has for some time been studying the possible reorganization of railroad maintenance forces and procedure. This proposal will be extended to all regions and not restricted to the Atlantic region.
The management goes on to say that, generally speaking, this reorganization, which contemplates the extension of territories cur-

rently worked by track forces, decreasing the number of gangs and increasing the size of some crews, will ultimately result in a reduction of staff requirements. However, in the Atlantic region, the hon. member will be glad to know it is not contemplated that this will cause any lay-offs of employees, as it is the intention to reduce the forces over a period of time through normal attrition.
Motion agreed to and the house adjourned at 10.23 p.m.

Tuesday, May 12, 1964
